title: Bianca: NUR 235 Health and Physical Assessment, Test 2 — Revised Version 2
description: Versioned revised 100-question practice bank prepared from the instructor-reviewed Bianca NUR 235 Test 2 candidate. This is a release asset for review and is not live until separately approved and deployed. Retains all question IDs and the 70 single-select/30 SATA distribution. Original question wording remains available in bianca-nur235-test2-bank.json.
source_basis: The five supplied NUR 235 lecture presentations: Assessment of the Eyes 2026; Assessment of the Head, Face 2026; Assessment of the Neck, Lymph and Thyroid, 2026; ENMT 2026; and Respiratory Assessment 2026. Ambiguous or inaccurate slide statements are qualified in the slide_review notes and are not used as keyed clinical facts.
difficulty_note: Moderate and challenging are author estimates, not empirically calibrated. Most questions require application of assessment findings, selection of a technique, or interpretation in context.

scoring.note: All and only the keyed answers earn one point. This is a practice scoring choice.

slide_review.issue: The slide describes a chalazion as an infection of the meibomian gland.
slide_review.clarification: A chalazion is usually a noninfectious obstructive inflammatory lesion; a hordeolum is an acute localized infection. The questions distinguish these findings.

slide_review.issue: The broad statement that conjunctivitis is highly contagious and that isolation practice is changing does not distinguish infectious from allergic causes or the care setting.
slide_review.clarification: Transmission precautions depend on likely cause, symptoms, and setting policy. The questions avoid treating all conjunctivitis as contagious or prescribing a universal isolation rule.

slide_review.issue: The statement that first-trimester headaches are relieved when hormone levels stabilize can imply a predictable benign course.
slide_review.clarification: Headache patterns vary. A new, sudden, severe, persistent, or neurologically accompanied headache during pregnancy requires assessment rather than reassurance based only on trimester.

slide_review.issue: The ancestry-based statement linking European ancestry to small teeth and increased decay risk is unsupported and overgeneralized.
slide_review.clarification: It is not used as a clinical premise. Questions focus on the individual patient's oral findings, history, and access needs.

slide_review.issue: The Rinne description gives a fixed 2:1 ratio in seconds, and the later slide equates any Weber lateralization with potential hearing loss without identifying the side or type.
slide_review.clarification: Rinne is interpreted qualitatively as air conduction greater than bone conduction in normal hearing, while Weber lateralization must be interpreted with the Rinne result and the clinical context.

slide_review.issue: The keyed response that right-sided Weber lateralization alone means potential hearing loss is nonspecific.
slide_review.clarification: Sound lateralizes toward the affected ear with conductive loss and toward the better ear with unilateral sensorineural loss; tuning-fork screening should be followed by appropriate hearing evaluation.

slide_review.issue: The older-adult respiratory rate range of 12–25 may normalize tachypnea if treated as an age-based normal range.
slide_review.clarification: The questions use the adult resting reference range of 12–20 breaths/minute as a screening reference and emphasize the patient's baseline, effort, symptoms, and overall context.

slide_review.issue: Describing asthma as due to allergens is too narrow; allergens are only one possible trigger and asthma is not invariably allergic.
slide_review.clarification: Questions treat triggers as individualized and include nonallergic triggers rather than implying a single cause.

slide_review.issue: The slide lists mechanical ventilation as a cause of pneumonia.
slide_review.clarification: Mechanical ventilation increases risk for ventilator-associated pneumonia; it is not an infectious cause. Aspiration can cause aspiration-related lung injury or infection, depending on the clinical context.

slide_review.issue: The phrase that listed chest-wall variations require intervention is not qualified by severity or clinical effect.
slide_review.clarification: Questions require assessment of severity, symptoms, function, and change from baseline rather than assuming every structural variation needs intervention.

slide_review.issue: The slide's respiratory-rate values are presented for broad age groups without enough detail about exact age, activity, sleep, or distress.
slide_review.clarification: Questions use the finding in a clinical context and do not treat one broad age-band value as a universal threshold.

questions.stem: A patient reports that vision in the right eye has become less clear. Which action best produces a valid distance-acuity comparison?

options.text: Test both eyes together at the chart's specified distance with usual correction, then record one Snellen fraction.
With usual corrective lenses on, test each eye separately at the chart's prescribed distance and document each result.
Test each eye separately without the patient's usual distance correction, then compare the results with the corrected baseline.
Test the right eye at a shorter distance and convert the result to the chart's standard distance without noting the change.

questions.correct_rationale: This item assesses distance visual acuity technique. Distance acuity is compared eye by eye at the chart's specified distance, using the patient's usual correction and preventing the uncovered eye from assisting. Document the result for each eye and note whether correction was worn.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: Testing both eyes together can conceal a unilateral deficit, and one combined fraction cannot compare the eyes.
option_rationales.B: Best choice: Testing each eye separately at the prescribed distance with usual correction gives a valid, comparable acuity measure.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: Removing usual distance correction changes the condition measured, so the result is not comparable with corrected baseline.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Changing chart distance changes Snellen testing conditions; an unreported conversion can misstate acuity.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: this item assesses distance visual acuity technique.

questions.stem: A patient reads 20/50 with the left eye. Which interpretation is accurate?

options.text: At 50 feet, the patient sees what a person with standard acuity sees at 20 feet.
At 20 feet, the patient reads the 20/20 line but has difficulty reading a near card.
At 20 feet, the patient reads what a person with standard acuity reads at 50 feet.
The result localizes the reduced acuity to the retina rather than simply describing visual performance.

questions.correct_rationale: The numerator is the testing distance and the denominator is the distance at which standard acuity reads the same line. Thus, 20/50 indicates reduced distance acuity; the fraction alone does not identify its cause.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: This reverses the Snellen fraction: 20/50 means testing at 20 feet, not 50 feet.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: This describes normal distance acuity plus a near-vision concern, which is not what 20/50 reports.
option_rationales.C: Best choice: The numerator is the testing distance and the denominator is the distance at which standard acuity reads that line.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: A Snellen fraction describes visual acuity; it does not identify a retinal cause.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: the numerator is the testing distance and the denominator is the distance at which standard acuity reads the same line.

questions.stem: During the six cardinal positions-of-gaze test, the patient's right eye fails to move laterally when looking toward the right. Which cranial nerve primarily supplies the muscle responsible for that movement?

options.text: Cranial nerve II
Cranial nerve III
Cranial nerve IV
Cranial nerve VI

questions.correct_rationale: Abduction of the eye is performed by the lateral rectus, supplied by cranial nerve VI (abducens). A new movement deficit should be documented and interpreted with onset, diplopia, pupils, and other neurologic findings.

option_rationales.A: Cranial nerve II carries visual sensory information; it does not innervate an extraocular muscle.
option_rationales.B: Cranial nerve III supplies most extraocular muscles, but not the lateral rectus.
option_rationales.C: Cranial nerve IV supplies the superior oblique muscle, not the lateral rectus.
option_rationales.D: Cranial nerve VI innervates the lateral rectus and produces abduction.

questions.exam_strategy: Link the movement deficit to the muscle before mapping it to the cranial nerve.

questions.stem: Which observations are expected when a patient with intact pupillary responses is assessed with a penlight and a near target? Select all that apply.

options.text: Both pupils dilate when light is directed into one eye.
The opposite pupil also constricts when light is directed into one eye.
The pupils constrict and the eyes converge when shifting focus from far to near.
Only the illuminated pupil should constrict; the other pupil should remain unchanged.
The pupil receiving the light constricts.

questions.correct_rationale: Direct and consensual constriction are expected to light, while a near response includes convergence and pupillary constriction. These are the normal responses assessed in the course eye examination.

option_rationales.A: Not appropriate: light normally causes direct and consensual constriction, not dilation.
option_rationales.B: Appropriate: the consensual response is constriction of the nonilluminated pupil.
option_rationales.C: Appropriate: pupillary constriction and convergence are components of the near response.
option_rationales.D: Not appropriate: an intact consensual response includes constriction of the opposite pupil.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: this is the direct pupillary light response.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: light in one eye produces direct constriction in the illuminated pupil and consensual constriction in the opposite pupil.

questions.stem: A penlight is held at midline while the patient looks straight ahead. The reflected light appears in the same location on both corneas. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: A symmetric reflection suggests normal acuity and peripheral fields in both eyes.
Symmetric reflections support aligned eye position in primary gaze but do not assess acuity or fields.
A symmetric reflex is enough to assess extraocular movement through each gaze position.
Assess the reflex while the patient follows the penlight through the six gaze positions.

questions.correct_rationale: A symmetric corneal light reflex supports alignment in primary gaze. It does not establish acuity, fields, or full extraocular movement.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: Corneal light symmetry screens alignment in primary gaze; it does not measure acuity or peripheral fields.
option_rationales.B: Best choice: Matching corneal reflections support symmetric alignment in primary gaze, without claiming to test acuity or fields.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: A corneal light reflex is a primary-gaze alignment screen, not assessment through the six cardinal gaze positions.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Following a target through cardinal positions assesses extraocular movement, not the stated static reflection finding.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: a symmetric corneal light reflex supports alignment in primary gaze.

questions.stem: A patient reports a sudden shower of new floaters, flashes of light, and a dark curtain moving across one visual field. What is the priority response?

options.text: Arrange urgent same-day ophthalmic evaluation and document the onset and affected field.
Reassure the patient that floaters commonly accompany aging and schedule routine follow-up.
Repeat the Snellen test tomorrow to determine whether the curtain resolves.
Apply a warm compress and reassess after the patient rests.

questions.correct_rationale: New flashes, floaters, and a curtain-like field defect can signal retinal detachment, a time-sensitive threat to vision. The priority is urgent eye evaluation, not delaying for routine testing or home treatment.

option_rationales.A: Prompt specialist assessment is appropriate for a new curtain or field defect with flashes/floaters.
option_rationales.B: Age-related floaters do not safely explain this acute combination of symptoms.
option_rationales.C: Waiting until tomorrow risks delaying treatment for a vision-threatening emergency.
option_rationales.D: A compress does not address a possible retinal emergency.

questions.exam_strategy: A sudden curtain or field loss is an urgent change, even when central acuity is not yet known.

questions.stem: A patient develops severe unilateral eye pain, blurred vision with colored halos, nausea, and a red eye. What is the priority response?

options.text: Complete acuity, field, and pupil testing in both eyes, then contact the receiving clinician with results.
Arrange routine eye evaluation later that day, and advise the patient to return sooner if vision worsens.
Use an over-the-counter redness-relief drop, reassess symptoms, and escalate only if they persist.
Initiate immediate emergency evaluation; obtain and communicate focused findings without delaying escalation.
Wait for the next routine appointment if the patient can still perceive light.

questions.correct_rationale: Severe unilateral pain, red eye, halos/blurred vision, and nausea are concerning for acute angle closure and require immediate emergency evaluation. Focused assessment supports handoff but must not delay escalation.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: A complete routine examination must not delay emergency evaluation of painful red eye with halos, nausea, and blurred vision.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: These acute symptoms may indicate a sight-threatening emergency; routine same-day scheduling is too slow.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: Redness-relief drops do not treat a possible acute pressure emergency and could delay definitive care.
option_rationales.D: Best choice: Perceiving light does not exclude acute angle closure or make waiting for routine care safe.
option_rationales.E: Not selected: Immediate emergency evaluation is needed; focused assessment and handoff should not delay escalation.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: severe unilateral pain, red eye, halos/blurred vision, and nausea are concerning for acute angle closure and require immediate emergency evaluation.

questions.stem: An older adult says that straight lines look wavy and the center of a page is missing, but can still notice objects approaching from the side. Which visual pattern best fits the report?

options.text: Central vision impairment, as can occur with macular degeneration.
Peripheral field loss typical of early chronic open-angle glaucoma.
A refractive error that can be confirmed from the symptom description alone.
Presbyopia, which characteristically creates a central scotoma.

questions.correct_rationale: Distortion and loss of central vision are characteristic concerns with macular disease. Preserved peripheral awareness does not exclude an ocular disorder; the patient needs appropriate eye evaluation.

option_rationales.A: Central distortion or a central blind area is consistent with macular involvement.
option_rationales.B: Glaucoma classically threatens peripheral fields, not a new central distortion as described.
option_rationales.C: Refraction can blur vision but does not safely explain a central scotoma or metamorphopsia.
option_rationales.D: Presbyopia affects near focusing and does not produce a central field defect.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the location and quality of the visual change to distinguish central from peripheral patterns.

questions.stem: A patient with long-standing diabetes denies vision changes and asks whether an eye examination is still necessary. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: A symptom-free history is enough to defer retinal screening until a new visual change is reported.
A normal pupil response is reassuring enough to choose a less frequent retinal-screening interval.
Yes. Early retinal changes may be silent; follow the dilated-exam interval recommended by the eye-care clinician.
A routine central-acuity check is a suitable substitute for a dilated retinal examination in an asymptomatic patient.

questions.correct_rationale: Early diabetic retinopathy may have no symptoms. Screening is therefore not replaced by a symptom-free report or a normal pupil response. The proposed wording appropriately refers to the patient's recommended schedule rather than making a new universal interval claim.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: Diabetic retinal disease may progress before symptoms appear, so symptom-free status is not a reason to defer screening.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: Pupil responses do not rule out retinal disease or determine an appropriate retinal-screening interval.
option_rationales.C: Best choice: Retinal screening remains important because early diabetic changes can be silent; follow the eye-care clinician’s dilated-exam schedule.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Central acuity testing does not visualize the retina and cannot replace a dilated retinal examination.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: early diabetic retinopathy may have no symptoms.

questions.concept: Contact-lens wearer with red painful eye
questions.stem: A contact-lens wearer reports a painful red eye with photophobia and blurred vision. Which nursing assessment or response is appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Allow continued lens wear if redness briefly improves after using an old prescription drop.
Arrange prompt eye-care evaluation for the painful, photophobic eye with blurred vision.
Tell the patient to remove the lens and avoid wearing it again until an eye-care clinician advises.
If it does not delay referral, assess and document visual acuity in each eye.
Ask when symptoms began, how lenses are used, and about discharge, injury, and visual change.

questions.correct_rationale: Pain, photophobia, and blurred vision in a contact-lens wearer warrant prompt eye evaluation. Focused history, stopping lens use, and visual-acuity assessment when it does not delay referral support safe triage.

option_rationales.A: Not appropriate: symptom improvement after an unverified medication does not rule out serious disease or make lens use safe.
option_rationales.B: Appropriate: contact-lens-related pain and visual change can signal corneal injury or infection and should not wait.
option_rationales.C: Appropriate: continued lens wear may worsen irritation or infection while evaluation is pending.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate: baseline acuity helps characterize the change, but urgent referral takes priority.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: these focused details help characterize a potentially sight-threatening red eye.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: pain, photophobia, and blurred vision in a contact-lens wearer require prompt assessment for potentially vision-threatening corneal disease.

questions.stem: A patient describes months of painless, gradual blurring and increasing glare while driving at night. Which finding is most consistent with this course?

options.text: Cataract-related lens opacity.
Acute angle-closure glaucoma.
Retinal detachment.
Acute bacterial conjunctivitis.

questions.correct_rationale: This item assesses cataract pattern. Cataracts commonly cause gradual, painless blurring and glare. The pattern warrants eye-care follow-up, while a sudden painful change or curtain-like defect would require urgent evaluation for another cause.

option_rationales.A: Best choice: Cataract commonly causes painless, gradual blurring and glare, including difficulty with night driving.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: Acute angle closure typically causes sudden severe pain and visual symptoms, not months of painless gradual change.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: Retinal detachment is generally acute, often with flashes, floaters, or curtain-like field loss.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Conjunctivitis usually causes surface redness or discharge; it does not fit months of gradual glare and blur.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: this item assesses cataract pattern.

questions.stem: A patient has bilateral itchy, watery eyes after yard work and no pain or vision change. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask about discharge, sick contacts, exposures, and whether one or both eyes are affected.
Use hand hygiene and avoid sharing towels or eye cosmetics while the cause is being clarified.
Redness alone does not distinguish allergic, viral, bacterial, or irritant conjunctivitis.
Do not recommend antibiotics solely because an eye is red; treatment depends on assessment of the likely cause.
Itching after yard work confirms allergy, so further assessment is unnecessary.

questions.correct_rationale: Itching after exposure may suggest allergy but does not establish the cause. Neutral history, infection-control precautions, and avoiding antibiotics based only on redness reflect the course focus on assessment before treatment.

option_rationales.A: Appropriate: these details help distinguish possible causes without diagnosing from one symptom.
option_rationales.B: Appropriate: these low-risk precautions reduce spread if an infectious cause is present.
option_rationales.C: Appropriate: appearance and history must be interpreted together; redness is nonspecific.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate: antibiotics do not treat allergic or viral causes and should not be selected from redness alone.
option_rationales.E: Not appropriate: exposure and itching support a possibility, not a confirmed etiology or a reason to skip assessment.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: itching and exposure support allergy as a possibility, not a confirmed diagnosis.

questions.concept: Absent red reflex in a child
questions.stem: During a child's eye assessment, the red reflex is absent in the left eye but present in the right. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Record the difference as a common variation if the child has no visual complaint or discomfort.
Use any normal distance-acuity result, if obtainable, as enough to dismiss the asymmetric reflex.
Ask whether it is a longstanding difference, and defer referral unless the caregiver reports a change.
Repeat the reflex assessment, compare both eyes, and arrange prompt evaluation.

questions.correct_rationale: An absent or asymmetric red reflex is an abnormal screening finding that requires prompt evaluation. A child need not be able to complete a Snellen chart or report symptoms for the finding to matter.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: An absent unilateral red reflex is abnormal even without symptoms and should not be dismissed as normal variation.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: A normal acuity measure cannot rule out the significance of an asymmetric or absent red reflex.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: Waiting for a reported change risks delaying evaluation of an abnormal reflex that may be clinically important.
option_rationales.D: Best choice: Repeat the assessment correctly, compare both eyes, and arrange prompt evaluation for an asymmetric reflex.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: an absent or asymmetric red reflex is an abnormal screening finding that requires prompt evaluation.

questions.stem: A patient reports bumping into objects on the left. Which technique best screens for a peripheral visual-field deficit at the bedside?

options.text: Have the patient read a distance chart with both eyes open and use the result to map the peripheral field.
Test one eye at a time and compare the patient's detection of a peripheral target with the examiner's field.
Test one eye at a time using a central near-vision card; central detail is the bedside screen for peripheral loss.
Compare direct pupillary constriction in each eye to identify the location of a peripheral-field defect.

questions.correct_rationale: Confrontation screening compares peripheral-target detection with the examiner while testing one eye at a time. Acuity and pupillary-response tests measure different functions.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: A distance chart primarily screens central acuity and does not map peripheral-field detection.
option_rationales.B: Best choice: Confrontation compares each eye’s peripheral target detection with the examiner’s field, directly screening for a deficit.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: A near-vision card assesses central near acuity, not the peripheral field implicated by bumping into objects.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Pupillary constriction assesses a reflex pathway, not the extent of peripheral visual fields.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: confrontation screening compares peripheral-target detection with the examiner while testing one eye at a time.

questions.stem: During an eye assessment, the nurse asks the patient to shift focus from a distant object to a near target. Which pupillary response is expected?

options.text: The pupils constrict as focus shifts to the near target.
The pupils remain unchanged because accommodation affects vision only.
The pupils dilate as the patient shifts focus to the near target.
Only the pupil in the eye viewing the near target constricts.

questions.correct_rationale: The lecture defines accommodation as the pupillary change when focusing from a distant to a near point; the pupils constrict with near focus.

option_rationales.A: Best choice: Near focus produces pupillary constriction as part of the accommodation response.
option_rationales.B: Accommodation includes a pupillary response; it is not limited to visual acuity.
option_rationales.C: Near focus does not normally cause pupillary dilation.
option_rationales.D: Accommodation is assessed by the pupil response to the near focus, not by constriction of only one eye.

questions.exam_strategy: Connect accommodation with the pupil's response when the patient shifts focus from far to near.

questions.stem: A patient with gradually worsening peripheral awareness says central reading vision remains clear and there has been no sudden pain. Which statements are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Chronic open-angle glaucoma can progress with peripheral-field loss while central reading vision remains clear.
A painless course rules out chronic open-angle glaucoma.
A normal central Snellen result can coexist with a peripheral-field defect.
This symptom pattern alone establishes chronic open-angle glaucoma.
Arrange a comprehensive eye examination with visual-field assessment; central acuity alone cannot exclude field loss.

questions.correct_rationale: Chronic open-angle glaucoma may cause peripheral-field loss before central acuity changes and may progress without severe pain. Comprehensive examination, including fields, is needed; a normal central acuity result cannot exclude field loss.

option_rationales.A: Appropriate: peripheral loss may precede central acuity change in chronic glaucoma.
option_rationales.B: Not appropriate: chronic open-angle glaucoma is often painless; absence of pain is not reassuring enough to exclude it.
option_rationales.C: Appropriate: central acuity testing does not measure the entire visual field.
option_rationales.D: Not appropriate: the pattern warrants evaluation but is not diagnostic without comprehensive examination.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: peripheral-field testing is needed to assess the reported change.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: chronic open-angle glaucoma may progress slowly, beginning with peripheral-field loss, and may be painless.

questions.stem: One patient has a tender, red bump at the eyelid margin; another has a firm, usually painless lump within the eyelid that has persisted for several weeks. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: The tender, red eyelid-margin lesion is more consistent with a chalazion; the persistent painless lump is more consistent with a hordeolum.
Both findings are caused by bacterial infection of an eyelid gland, differing mainly in duration.
Most eyelid lesions resolve, so persistence is less relevant than tenderness when deciding on evaluation.
A tender, acute eyelid-margin lesion fits a hordeolum; a persistent, usually painless lump within the lid fits a chalazion.

questions.correct_rationale: A hordeolum is typically an acute, tender localized infection. A chalazion is usually a chronic, noninfectious inflammatory lump related to gland obstruction. Persistent, recurrent, or vision-affecting lesions need evaluation. This wording preserves the existing clinical correction to the lecture's overstatement that chalazia are infections.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: The descriptions are reversed: an acute tender lid-margin lesion is typical of hordeolum; a chalazion is often persistent and painless.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: A chalazion is usually an obstructed gland rather than an acute bacterial infection; the lesions differ by more than duration.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: Persistence matters, especially for a lump lasting weeks; tenderness alone does not determine need for evaluation.
option_rationales.D: Best choice: An acute tender lid-margin lesion fits hordeolum; a persistent, usually painless lump within the lid fits chalazion.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: a hordeolum is typically an acute, tender localized infection.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to inspect a patient's fundus with an ophthalmoscope. Which actions improve the assessment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the room brightly lit so the pupils remain constricted throughout the examination.
Explain the close approach before bringing the ophthalmoscope near the patient.
Ask the patient to follow the ophthalmoscope as it moves across the fundus.
Use the examiner’s right eye and hand for the patient’s right eye, and the left eye and hand for the left; approach temporally.
Ask the patient to keep gaze on a distant fixed point while the fundus is viewed.

questions.correct_rationale: Fundoscopy is easier when the patient is prepared, fixes gaze on a distant target, and the examiner uses the corresponding eye/hand while approaching from the temporal side. These are course-aligned examination techniques.

option_rationales.A: Not appropriate: dimmer ambient light generally facilitates fundus viewing; constricted pupils make visualization harder.
option_rationales.B: Appropriate: explaining the maneuver reduces surprise and supports cooperation.
option_rationales.C: Not appropriate: the patient should maintain gaze on a distant fixed target rather than track the instrument.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate: matching eye and hand and approaching from the temporal side support a controlled funduscopic view.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: steady distant fixation helps keep the eyes positioned for examination.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: explain the close approach, align the examiner's eye and hand with the side being examined, and have the patient maintain distant fixation.

questions.stem: During an older adult's eye inspection, the nurse sees a gray-white ring at the corneal periphery. The patient denies pain and visual change. Which response is best?

options.text: A cataract-related opacity within the lens, usually seen as clouding through the pupil.
A pinguecula, a localized conjunctival change beside the cornea rather than a corneal ring.
Corneal arcus, a gray-white ring at the corneal edge that can be age-associated in older adults.
A corneal abrasion, a surface injury that can appear as a complete gray-white peripheral ring.

questions.correct_rationale: Arcus is a gray-white peripheral corneal ring and may be age-associated. Document its location and interpret it in context; the finding does not by itself explain a separate visual complaint.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: A cataract is lens opacity behind the pupil, not a peripheral ring at the corneal edge.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: A pinguecula is a localized conjunctival elevation beside the cornea, not a gray-white corneal ring.
option_rationales.C: Best choice: A peripheral gray-white corneal ring in an older adult is consistent with age-associated corneal arcus.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: An abrasion is a corneal surface injury and does not present as an age-associated circumferential peripheral ring.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: arcus is a gray-white peripheral corneal ring and may be age-associated.

questions.stem: A patient reports a sudden visual change that is being urgently escalated. Which nursing actions support the handoff without delaying evaluation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask the patient to drive to the clinic if vision begins to improve.
Complete a full routine eye examination before notifying the receiving clinician.
Describe which eye is affected and the portion of the visual field involved.
Report associated flashes, floaters, pain, redness, halos, nausea, and any acuity findings already obtained.
Document when the change began and whether it was sudden, intermittent, or worsening.

questions.correct_rationale: A concise handoff for a sudden visual change includes timing, laterality/field, and associated symptoms or measurements already obtained. Communicate promptly without delaying urgent evaluation.

option_rationales.A: Not appropriate: visual change can recur or worsen, and impaired vision makes self-driving unsafe.
option_rationales.B: Not appropriate: a routine examination should not delay escalation of a sudden visual change.
option_rationales.C: Appropriate: laterality and field location make the handoff more clinically useful.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate: associated symptoms and existing findings help characterize the urgent change.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: onset and course help the receiving clinician assess urgency and differential.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: onset, affected eye/field, associated symptoms, and available acuity findings support urgent handoff.

questions.stem: A patient reports a recurring headache. Which follow-up question best characterizes the symptom before the nurse interprets it?

options.text: Has this same headache happened before, and what did you do for it?
Would you describe the pain as a migraine so I can document the likely cause?
When did it begin, where is it, what does it feel like, and what changes it?
Would you prefer medication before we discuss the headache pattern?

questions.correct_rationale: An open, structured history characterizes the symptom without leading the patient or assigning a cause before assessment.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: Prior episodes and self-care response can help, but do not first characterize onset, location, quality, and modifiers.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: Calling it migraine presumes a diagnosis instead of eliciting the headache characteristics.
option_rationales.C: Best choice: Onset, site, quality, and aggravating or relieving factors are focused descriptors needed before interpretation.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Offering medication before characterizing the symptom skips assessment needed to guide safe care.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: an open, structured history characterizes the symptom without leading the patient or assigning a cause before assessment.

questions.stem: During scalp palpation, the patient identifies a small tender area that was not visible on inspection. What should the nurse do next?

options.text: Note the tenderness, but defer further description until the next routine scalp examination.
Record the site and its features, ask about onset or injury, and compare gently with nearby scalp.
Label the tender spot a cyst based on its small size, then document that likely benign cause.
Press firmly several times to decide whether the tender spot is superficial or extends deeper.

questions.correct_rationale: Gentle description and relevant history are appropriate; the nurse should not diagnose from palpation alone or cause unnecessary pain.

option_rationales.A: This delays documenting a newly reported finding and omits details that may guide follow-up.
option_rationales.B: Best choice: It documents the finding and relevant history without presuming a diagnosis or causing unnecessary pain.
option_rationales.C: Size and tenderness do not establish a cyst; the nurse should describe findings rather than infer a diagnosis.
option_rationales.D: Repeated firm pressure may increase pain and is not needed for a safe initial description.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: gentle description and relevant history are appropriate; the nurse should not diagnose from palpation alone or cause unnecessary pain.

questions.stem: A patient reports discomfort near the jaw joint. Which maneuver best assesses temporomandibular joint movement?

options.text: Ask the patient to open and close the jaw and move it laterally; note pain or limitation.
Ask the patient to raise both eyebrows and smile; note symmetry of facial movement.
Ask the patient to rotate the head and shrug the shoulders; note range and symmetry.
Ask the patient to follow a target through the six fields of gaze; note eye movement.

questions.correct_rationale: The lecture describes testing temporomandibular-joint range of motion; asking the patient to open, close, and move the jaw laterally assesses movement and symptoms.

option_rationales.A: Best choice: Opening, closing, and lateral jaw movement assess joint motion while allowing the nurse to note symptoms.
option_rationales.B: This observes facial expression rather than temporomandibular-joint movement.
option_rationales.C: These movements assess the neck and shoulder, not the jaw joint.
option_rationales.D: Following a visual target assesses ocular movement, not jaw-joint function.

questions.exam_strategy: Assess the TMJ while the patient moves the jaw; do not force movement against resistance.

questions.stem: Which instructions assess symmetric facial movement mediated primarily by cranial nerve VII? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask the patient to smile and show the teeth.
Ask the patient to raise both eyebrows.
Ask the patient to protrude the tongue and move it side to side.
Compare light-touch sensation on each cheek.
Ask the patient to close both eyes tightly while gently testing closure.

questions.correct_rationale: CN VII motor function is assessed by comparing facial movements such as smiling, raising the eyebrows, and tightly closing the eyes. Tongue movement and facial sensation test other functions.

option_rationales.A: Appropriate: smiling assesses symmetric lower facial movement mediated primarily by CN VII.
option_rationales.B: Appropriate: forehead movement assesses CN VII motor function.
option_rationales.C: Not appropriate for CN VII: tongue movement primarily assesses CN XII.
option_rationales.D: Not appropriate for CN VII motor function: facial sensation is primarily assessed through CN V.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: forceful eye closure assesses CN VII motor function.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: smile, eyebrow raise, and tight eye closure assess CN VII motor function.

questions.stem: A patient reports jaw clicking and discomfort when chewing. Which assessment is most appropriate?

options.text: Inspect the teeth and gums for caries or inflammation, then ask whether chewing worsens discomfort.
Palpate the temporal arteries and ask about headache or scalp tenderness near the jaw.
Observe and gently palpate both TMJs during opening and closing; assess motion, pain, and clicking.
Observe facial symmetry during smiling, then ask about recent weakness or numbness.

questions.correct_rationale: The TMJ should be assessed during movement and not forced. Carotid auscultation and oral inspection do not answer the reported joint symptom.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: A static oral inspection does not assess jaw-joint movement that produces clicking and chewing discomfort.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: Forceful opening against resistance may worsen pain and is not the appropriate initial assessment of symptomatic TMJ.
option_rationales.C: Best choice: Gentle palpation during jaw movement assesses joint motion and reported pain or clicking.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Carotid auscultation evaluates vascular sounds, not the source of jaw-joint clicking.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: the TMJ should be assessed during movement and not forced.

questions.concept: Acute facial weakness and stroke recognition
questions.stem: A patient's family reports that the patient's face suddenly became asymmetric 20 minutes ago. The nurse also observes new arm drift and slurred speech. What is the priority action?

options.text: Complete a full cranial-nerve examination before contacting the response team.
Activate the facility stroke response and establish the last-known-well time.
Ask the patient to rest while a second nurse repeats the assessment in an hour.
Request a routine outpatient evaluation after documenting possible Bell’s palsy.

questions.correct_rationale: Sudden facial asymmetry with arm drift and speech change warrants immediate stroke evaluation. Do not delay the emergency response for a comprehensive exam or assign a diagnosis.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: A full examination would delay response to sudden facial asymmetry with arm drift and slurred speech.
option_rationales.B: Best choice: Sudden focal neurologic findings require immediate stroke activation; last-known-well informs time-sensitive treatment.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: Waiting an hour risks delaying treatment for possible acute stroke.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Bell’s palsy does not explain accompanying arm drift and slurred speech; outpatient referral is unsafe.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: sudden facial asymmetry with arm drift and speech change warrants immediate stroke evaluation.

questions.stem: A patient reports a headache during a focused head-and-face assessment. Which details should the nurse ask about? Select all that apply.

options.text: When it began and whether the pain has changed since onset.
Where the pain is located and how the patient describes it.
Whether dizziness, visual changes, or other symptoms occur with it.
What makes it better or worse and what the patient has tried.
Assume a familiar headache has the same cause and skip current symptom questions.

questions.correct_rationale: The lecture's focused headache history includes onset, description, associated symptoms, and relevant context. Gathering these details supports assessment without assuming the cause.

option_rationales.A: Appropriate: onset and change over time help characterize the headache.
option_rationales.B: Appropriate: location and the patient's description are central symptom-history details.
option_rationales.C: Appropriate: associated symptoms such as dizziness or visual changes add relevant assessment context.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate: aggravating and relieving factors and prior actions help characterize the complaint.
option_rationales.E: Not appropriate: a familiar history does not replace asking about the current episode and any changes.

questions.exam_strategy: For a focused headache history, ask about onset and course, location and description, associated symptoms, and aggravating or relieving factors.

questions.stem: A patient reports a new headache and tenderness over the temple. Which response best applies the head-and-face assessment techniques from the lecture?

options.text: Ask about onset and associated symptoms, assess the temporal area gently, and report the finding.
Ask about onset and prior headaches, then reassure because vision is currently unchanged.
Assess jaw movement and tenderness at the TMJ, then document that finding.
Document a temporal-artery disorder based on tenderness without further assessment.

questions.correct_rationale: The lecture supports focused headache questions and inspection/palpation of the head and temporal area. Document the observed tenderness and communicate a new finding without assigning a cause.

option_rationales.A: Best choice: It gathers symptom context, assesses gently, and communicates the finding without overdiagnosis.
option_rationales.B: Prior headache history is relevant, but unchanged vision does not make a new tender headache safe to dismiss.
option_rationales.C: TMJ assessment is useful for jaw-joint symptoms but does not characterize the reported temporal tenderness.
option_rationales.D: Tenderness alone does not establish a vascular diagnosis; additional assessment and clinical evaluation are needed.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the taught focused history and gentle head/temporal-area assessment; document findings rather than infer a diagnosis.

questions.stem: A pregnant patient in the first trimester reports a new severe headache unlike prior headaches and brief blurred vision. Which response is best?

options.text: Assess onset, blood pressure, visual and neurologic symptoms, then promptly notify the appropriate clinician.
Use the trimester to classify the headache as expected and defer additional assessment.
Recommend an over-the-counter medication before checking the patient's history or pregnancy plan.
Schedule routine follow-up unless the headache remains after hormone levels stabilize.

questions.correct_rationale: The lecture's first-trimester statement does not explain away a new severe headache with visual symptoms. Prompt assessment is appropriate; medication choices must be individualized in pregnancy.

option_rationales.A: Best choice: A new severe headache with visual symptoms in pregnancy needs focused assessment and prompt clinician notification.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: Pregnancy does not make a severe atypical headache with blurred vision an expected symptom to defer.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: Medication advice before assessment may be unsafe during pregnancy and does not address warning symptoms.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Waiting for hormonal changes to resolve could delay care for a serious cause of new headache and visual symptoms.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: the lecture's first-trimester statement does not explain away a new severe headache with visual symptoms.

questions.stem: During an infant assessment, the anterior fontanel appears persistently bulging while the infant is calm and held upright. The infant is also unusually difficult to arouse. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Document the finding, recheck shortly, and notify the clinician if it remains unchanged.
Consider molding after checking position, but defer escalation unless another finding appears.
Ask about recent feeding and illness, then observe at home before arranging follow-up.
Escalate the persistent bulge and decreased arousability; assess neurologic status and vital signs.

questions.correct_rationale: A persistently bulging fontanel in a calm, upright infant with decreased responsiveness warrants prompt medical evaluation. Do not press forcefully or delay escalation.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: A persistently bulging fontanel with decreased arousability is concerning and should not wait for routine follow-up.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: Molding does not explain away a persistent bulge and reduced arousability in a calm, upright infant.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: Home observation until tomorrow delays evaluation of a potentially urgent neurologic finding.
option_rationales.D: Best choice: A persistent bulge with reduced arousability warrants prompt escalation and assessment.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: a persistently bulging fontanel in a calm, upright infant with decreased responsiveness warrants prompt medical evaluation.

questions.stem: Which actions are part of the head-and-face assessment described in the lecture? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inspect head shape and scalp, and palpate gently for masses or tenderness.
Infer the patient's mood from facial expression without asking how they feel.
Observe facial symmetry and note any abnormal facial movements.
Diagnose the cause of a headache from the location of pain alone.
Ask about headache, dizziness, loss of consciousness, or head injury.

questions.correct_rationale: The lecture describes head/scalp inspection and palpation, observation of facial symmetry and movement, and focused questions about headache, dizziness, loss of consciousness, and injury.

option_rationales.A: Appropriate: inspection and gentle palpation of the head and scalp are listed assessment techniques.
option_rationales.B: Not appropriate: facial expression should be observed and described; it does not establish the patient's mood.
option_rationales.C: Appropriate: facial symmetry and movement are part of the focused assessment.
option_rationales.D: Not appropriate: pain location is one history detail and does not establish a headache diagnosis.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: these are examples of the lecture's focused head-assessment questions.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the lecture's assessment sequence: inspect and palpate the head/scalp, observe the face, and obtain a focused history.

questions.stem: A pregnant patient reports sudden facial and hand swelling with a persistent headache and new visual spots. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Promptly assess blood pressure and associated symptoms and notify the obstetric clinician.
Treat the swelling as routine pregnancy edema and defer assessment unless it becomes painful.
Document melasma as the explanation for swelling and visual spots.
Recommend limiting fluids and reassessing at the next routine visit.

questions.correct_rationale: Sudden facial/hand swelling with persistent headache and new visual symptoms needs prompt assessment for hypertensive or other urgent complications. Do not attribute edema to melasma or advise unprescribed fluid restriction.

option_rationales.A: Best choice: Sudden swelling with persistent headache and visual spots in pregnancy can indicate a serious hypertensive complication; check BP and promptly notify obstetric care.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: Facial and hand swelling with neurologic/visual symptoms should not be dismissed as routine edema.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: Melasma causes pigmentation, not swelling or visual spots, and cannot account for this warning-symptom cluster.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Fluid restriction and delayed reassessment do not evaluate possible obstetric danger signs.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: sudden facial/hand swelling with persistent headache and new visual symptoms needs prompt assessment for hypertensive or other urgent complications.

questions.stem: A patient has limited spontaneous facial movement but says they feel well. What is the best nursing response?

options.text: Describe movement, establish baseline, and avoid inferring mood.
Document depression because reduced facial movement indicates a low mood.
Diagnose an acute neurologic event from limited movement without checking onset.
Omit the finding because the patient reports feeling well.

questions.correct_rationale: The lecture directs the nurse to observe facial features and abnormal movements. Objective description and comparison with the patient's baseline avoid assigning an unsupported emotional or medical diagnosis.

option_rationales.A: Best choice: It describes the finding, establishes baseline, and avoids inferring mood from appearance.
option_rationales.B: Facial movement alone does not establish depression or the patient's emotional state.
option_rationales.C: An observed difference requires onset and context; it does not by itself establish a diagnosis.
option_rationales.D: Objective facial findings should be documented even when the patient reports feeling well.

questions.exam_strategy: Observe and describe facial movement, compare with baseline, and ask the patient rather than infer mood.

questions.stem: A patient has subtle facial asymmetry, and no baseline description is available. Which assessment steps are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask when the asymmetry began and whether it is new or changing.
Observe the face at rest and during smile, eyebrow raise, and eye closure.
Assess for associated speech, limb-strength, sensation, vision, or alertness changes.
Document the finding as a stroke before establishing onset or assessing associated symptoms.
Compare with prior descriptions or photographs when available and document the observed movement.

questions.correct_rationale: When baseline is unknown, determine onset, observe facial movement, assess associated neurologic changes, and compare with prior descriptions when available. Describe findings objectively rather than labeling a diagnosis prematurely.

option_rationales.A: Appropriate: onset and progression distinguish an acute change from a longstanding finding.
option_rationales.B: Appropriate: comparing several movements characterizes the asymmetry.
option_rationales.C: Appropriate: associated deficits may indicate an urgent neurologic problem.
option_rationales.D: Not appropriate: a nurse should report objective findings and not assign a diagnosis from appearance alone.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: baseline comparison and objective documentation clarify whether the finding is new.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: establish onset/baseline, characterize movement, and assess for associated neurologic findings.

questions.stem: A patient reports tenderness at the temple during a focused head assessment. Which action is appropriate?

options.text: Palpate the temporal artery gently and document the side and tenderness.
Inspect the oral mucosa and document any visible lesions.
Observe the temporomandibular joints while the patient opens and closes the jaw.
Observe facial symmetry during a smile and eyebrow raise.

questions.correct_rationale: The lecture includes inspection and palpation of the head and scalp, including the temporal artery. Gently assessing and objectively documenting the reported tender location is within the focused examination.

option_rationales.A: Best choice: Gentle temporal-artery palpation and side-specific documentation address the reported tenderness.
option_rationales.B: Oral inspection is useful in an oral complaint but does not assess the reported temporal tenderness.
option_rationales.C: TMJ movement is assessed for jaw-joint symptoms; it does not directly assess the tender temporal area.
option_rationales.D: Facial symmetry is relevant to movement but does not characterize the reported tenderness.

questions.exam_strategy: Use gentle, focused palpation and document the location and characteristics of tenderness.

questions.stem: A caregiver reports that an infant's head shape has become more asymmetric over several weeks. Which next step best supports an accurate assessment?

options.text: Measure head circumference once and use that value alone to identify the cause of the changing shape.
Reassure the caregiver that worsening asymmetry over several weeks is ordinary molding after birth.
Press on the cranial sutures to see whether pressure can correct the infant’s head shape.
Review birth and positioning history, inspect the shape and sutures, trend head circumference, and report progression.

questions.correct_rationale: Interpret infant head shape in developmental and birth context; trend objective measurements and report progression. Avoid forceful manipulation or conclusions from a single measure.

option_rationales.A: A single measurement cannot explain progressive asymmetry; trend measurements and assess other findings.
option_rationales.B: Progressive change should not be dismissed as molding; it needs an age-appropriate assessment.
option_rationales.C: Pressure on the sutures will not establish the cause and is not an appropriate assessment maneuver.
option_rationales.D: Best choice: It combines history, inspection, serial measurement, and follow-up for a progressive change.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: interpret infant head shape in developmental and birth context; trend objective measurements and report progression.

questions.stem: Which findings may be observed as part of an older adult's head-and-face assessment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reduced subcutaneous facial fullness.
New unilateral facial weakness should be assumed to be a normal age change.
Changes in hair, such as texture or distribution.
Tooth loss or other changes in dentition.
Some limitation in range of motion.

questions.correct_rationale: Reduced facial fullness, changes in hair and dentition, and some limitation in range of motion may be observed with aging. New unilateral facial weakness is not a normal age change and needs assessment.

option_rationales.A: Appropriate: loss of subcutaneous tissue can be an age-associated head-and-face change.
option_rationales.B: Not appropriate: new focal weakness is not a normal aging finding and requires prompt assessment.
option_rationales.C: Appropriate: hair changes may occur with aging, but a new focal change still needs context.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate: dentition can change with age and should be included in assessment.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: age-associated musculoskeletal changes may limit range, while new or painful limitation still needs evaluation.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: the slide 9 lifespan content lists loss of subcutaneous facial fat, hair changes, tooth loss, and range-of-motion limitations.

questions.stem: During an older-adult head-and-face assessment, the nurse notes gradual loss of subcutaneous facial fullness and changes in hair. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: These may occur with aging; document them, compare with baseline, and ask about related concerns.
They are age-related and need no comparison with the patient's previous appearance.
They are expected in older adults, so documentation is unnecessary when the patient feels well.
They indicate an acute neurologic change even when gradual and unchanged.

questions.correct_rationale: Slide 9 lists age-related changes in facial subcutaneous fat and hair. Document findings in context; age alone neither proves a diagnosis nor makes every change benign.

option_rationales.A: Best choice: These may accompany aging; compare with baseline and assess any related concerns.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: These nonspecific gradual changes do not establish a neurologic diagnosis.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: Age-associated does not mean irrelevant; document and assess changes in the person’s context.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: A gradual, unchanged appearance is not by itself evidence of acute stroke.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: slide 9 lists age-related changes in facial subcutaneous fat and hair.

questions.stem: During assessment, the right nasolabial fold appears flatter and the right corner of the mouth moves less during a smile. Which documentation is best?

options.text: Document right facial-nerve paralysis and Bell’s palsy based only on the asymmetric smile.
Document reduced right lower-face movement during smiling and assess onset, baseline, and associated findings.
Record that the patient may be uncooperative because the smile is not symmetrical on request.
Chart the face as normal because the patient can speak, despite reduced movement during smiling.

questions.correct_rationale: The best charting is objective, side-specific, and neutral. Diagnosis requires clinical evaluation; speech alone does not exclude facial weakness.

option_rationales.A: An asymmetric smile is a finding, not proof of paralysis or Bell’s palsy; assess onset and associated signs.
option_rationales.B: Best choice: It records the observable finding and prompts assessment without assigning an unsupported cause.
option_rationales.C: A difference in facial movement does not establish unwillingness; document the observed movement objectively.
option_rationales.D: Speech does not rule out facial asymmetry; document the movement finding and assess further.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: the best charting is objective, side-specific, and neutral.

questions.stem: A pregnant patient in the first trimester reports a mild headache similar to a familiar pattern that improves with rest. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Attribute the headache to pregnancy without asking about onset, associated symptoms, or changes from baseline.
Characterize onset, duration, severity, pattern, and response to usual measures.
Reassure the patient that all first-trimester headaches resolve when hormone levels stabilize.
Ask about visual changes, focal neurologic symptoms, blood-pressure concerns, and other warning features.
Review the pregnancy-specific care plan and medication history; seek guidance for new, worsening, or concerning symptoms.

questions.correct_rationale: A familiar mild first-trimester headache still merits focused history and screening for warning features. Review pregnancy-specific care and medication guidance; do not assume all headaches are benign or give unverified medication advice.

option_rationales.A: Not appropriate: pregnancy can contribute to symptoms but does not remove the need to assess the headache.
option_rationales.B: Appropriate: focused history identifies change from baseline and response to self-care.
option_rationales.C: Not appropriate: this overgeneralizes and could delay assessment of a new or concerning headache.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate: screening for warning signs helps determine whether prompt escalation is needed.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: medication decisions in pregnancy should be individualized and concerning symptoms assessed.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: a familiar, mild symptom without new warning features differs from the urgent presentations in #029 and #032, but still merits focused assessment.

questions.stem: During a routine neck inspection, the trachea appears slightly left of midline. The patient is comfortable and has no respiratory symptoms. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Diagnose tension pneumothorax from the initial visual impression.
Press firmly on the trachea until it appears centered.
Ignore the finding because tracheal position is not clinically relevant.
Reposition and reinspect, palpate gently, and compare with symptoms and baseline.

questions.correct_rationale: Verify a subtle observation before labeling it; acute deviation with distress is a different, urgent presentation.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: A visual impression alone does not establish pneumothorax, especially without respiratory symptoms.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: Forceful pressure is not a safe or valid way to reposition the trachea.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: Tracheal position is clinically relevant; an apparent deviation should be verified and interpreted in context.
option_rationales.D: Best choice: Repositioning and gentle reassessment distinguish position or normal variation from persistent deviation; symptoms and baseline guide interpretation.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: verify a subtle observation before labeling it; acute deviation with distress is a different, urgent presentation.

questions.stem: Which technique is most appropriate when palpating the cervical lymph-node groups?

options.text: Use the thumb to press firmly into each node until its borders are clear.
Palpate each node group gently with finger pads in circular motions and compare both sides.
Assess only the supraclavicular group because other cervical nodes cannot be palpated.
Pinch each node sharply between the fingertips to test consistency.

questions.correct_rationale: Gentle, systematic palpation supports comparison and characterization without unnecessary discomfort.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: Firm thumb pressure can cause discomfort and is less controlled than gentle node palpation with finger pads.
option_rationales.B: Best choice: Gentle circular finger-pad palpation by node group and side-to-side comparison supports systematic assessment.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: Other cervical groups can be assessed; restricting examination to supraclavicular nodes misses relevant findings.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Pinching sharply can cause pain and does not improve node characterization.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: gentle, systematic palpation supports comparison and characterization without unnecessary discomfort.

questions.stem: The nurse is observing the anterior neck for thyroid enlargement. Which instruction best helps the nurse observe thyroid movement?

options.text: Ask the patient to turn the head against resistance while watching the thyroid.
Ask the patient to cough repeatedly while the nurse palpates both carotids.
Ask the patient to take a sip of water and swallow while observing the lower anterior neck.
Ask the patient to hold the breath and shrug both shoulders.

questions.correct_rationale: The thyroid region moves with swallowing; the other maneuvers do not assess that movement.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: Head rotation against resistance tests neck muscles, not thyroid movement with swallowing.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: Coughing and carotid palpation do not expose thyroid movement and add unnecessary procedures.
option_rationales.C: Best choice: The thyroid normally moves with swallowing, making a sip of water and observation the direct maneuver.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Breath holding and shoulder shrug do not assess thyroid movement.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: the thyroid region moves with swallowing; the other maneuvers do not assess that movement.

questions.stem: A cervical node is palpable. Which features should the nurse document to characterize it? Select all that apply.

options.text: Location and approximate size.
Tenderness and consistency.
Mobility or fixation relative to surrounding tissue.
Distribution, nearby node involvement, and relevant associated symptoms.
Label the node malignant based only on its size and texture.

questions.correct_rationale: Document objective node features such as location, size, tenderness, consistency, mobility, and distribution with associated symptoms. Palpation describes a finding but cannot establish malignancy.

option_rationales.A: Appropriate: these objective descriptors establish where the node is and its scale.
option_rationales.B: Appropriate: tenderness and texture are relevant findings to document without treating them as diagnostic.
option_rationales.C: Appropriate: mobility is a useful descriptive feature and may affect the need for follow-up.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate: pattern and context help the clinician interpret the finding.
option_rationales.E: Not appropriate: palpation characteristics may raise concern but do not diagnose malignancy.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: record objective node characteristics and context; palpation alone does not diagnose malignancy.

questions.stem: A patient reports chronic neck stiffness. Which assessment instruction is safest?

options.text: Move the patient’s head passively through full range before asking whether movement causes pain.
Use rapid repeated neck circles to test endurance and identify the direction of stiffness.
Assess rotation only, since flexion, extension, and lateral bending are not needed for neck range.
Have the patient flex, extend, rotate, and bend laterally within comfort; stop if pain occurs.

questions.correct_rationale: Active movement within comfort preserves patient control and avoids forcing a painful or symptomatic neck.

option_rationales.A: Ask about symptoms first and use active movement; passive movement may cause avoidable pain.
option_rationales.B: Rapid circles are not a controlled range-of-motion assessment and may aggravate symptoms.
option_rationales.C: A complete neck range assessment includes comfortable flexion, extension, rotation, and lateral bending.
option_rationales.D: Best choice: Active movement within comfort assesses range while limiting worsening symptoms.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: active movement within comfort preserves patient control and avoids forcing a painful or symptomatic neck.

questions.stem: A patient suddenly becomes severely short of breath after a central-line procedure. The nurse notes unilateral absent breath sounds, falling oxygen saturation, and tracheal deviation. What is the priority?

options.text: Activate emergency help and support immediate evaluation for a life-threatening complication.
Repeat the complete neck examination before activating the emergency response.
Reposition the patient and wait for the next scheduled oxygen-saturation measurement.
Attribute the deviation to anatomy because the patient had a central-line procedure.

questions.correct_rationale: Acute respiratory distress, unilateral absent breath sounds, falling oxygenation, and tracheal deviation after a central-line procedure require immediate escalation. Do not delay for a complete routine exam.

option_rationales.A: Best choice: Acute dyspnea, hypoxemia, unilateral absent sounds, and deviation after a line procedure suggest a life-threatening complication; activate emergency help.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: Repeating a complete neck examination delays urgent response to respiratory deterioration.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: Waiting for a scheduled measurement is unsafe with severe new dyspnea and falling oxygen saturation.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: New deviation with unilateral absent sounds and hypoxemia is not safely dismissed as anatomy.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: acute respiratory distress, unilateral absent breath sounds, falling oxygenation, and tracheal deviation after a central-line procedure require immediate escalation.

questions.stem: During a neck assessment, which actions are appropriate when observing the carotid arteries and jugular veins? Select all that apply.

options.text: Observe the neck vessels and compare visible carotid pulsations for symmetry.
Observe the jugular veins and describe visible venous pulsations.
Document the patient's position and communicate an unexpected visible finding.
Compress both carotid arteries at once to compare the visible pulsations.
Diagnose a vascular disorder from neck appearance without further assessment.

questions.correct_rationale: The lecture identifies observation of the carotid arteries and jugular veins as part of the neck assessment. Compare and describe visible findings, then communicate an unexpected observation without diagnosing from appearance alone.

option_rationales.A: Appropriate: the presentation includes observation of the carotid arteries; comparing describes visible symmetry.
option_rationales.B: Appropriate: the jugular veins are included in the lecture's neck-vessel observation.
option_rationales.C: Appropriate: documenting position and communicating an unexpected finding preserves context without diagnosing.
option_rationales.D: Not appropriate: compressing both carotids is unsafe and is not an observation technique.
option_rationales.E: Not appropriate: visual observation alone does not establish a vascular diagnosis.

questions.exam_strategy: Observe the carotid arteries and jugular veins, describe what is seen, and communicate unexpected findings.
