questions.stem: At 45 degrees, the nurse observes a sustained jugular venous column above the sternal angle in a patient with orthopnea. What is the best next step?

options.text: Document the column as expected at 45 degrees and continue the focused neck examination.
Raise the head of bed, document breathing status, and notify the clinician at the next routine round.
Document position and venous findings, assess cardiopulmonary status, and promptly notify the clinician.
Lower the head of bed for a repeat measurement, then resume routine care if the column decreases.

questions.correct_rationale: Describe the finding and position, assess the full clinical picture, and communicate the concerning pattern without unsafe manipulation.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: A sustained venous column above the sternal angle at 45 degrees is not simply an expected finding.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: A later routine report delays communication of a concerning finding in a patient with orthopnea.
option_rationales.C: Best choice: Document the position and finding, assess cardiopulmonary status, and promptly communicate the pattern.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Lowering the head of bed may worsen orthopnea; a decrease in the column does not make the reported symptoms safe to dismiss.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: describe the finding and position, assess the full clinical picture, and communicate the concerning pattern without unsafe manipulation.

questions.stem: A patient has visible anterior-neck fullness that rises during swallowing. The patient also reports new difficulty swallowing solid food. What is the best response?

options.text: Classify the fullness as normal because the thyroid region rises during swallowing.
Document the enlargement and new dysphagia and arrange further clinical evaluation.
Press deeply on the gland to reproduce the swallowing difficulty.
Diagnose a specific thyroid hormone disorder from appearance alone.

questions.correct_rationale: Thyroid movement with swallowing can be observed, but visible enlargement with new difficulty swallowing requires further evaluation.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: Movement with swallowing can be normal, but fullness plus new dysphagia needs evaluation rather than reassurance.
option_rationales.B: Best choice: Documenting enlargement and compressive symptom and arranging evaluation avoids overdiagnosis while addressing the finding.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: Deep pressure to reproduce dysphagia is unnecessary and may worsen discomfort.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Appearance and swallowing symptoms alone cannot identify a specific thyroid hormone disorder.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: thyroid movement with swallowing can be observed, but visible enlargement with new difficulty swallowing requires further evaluation.

questions.stem: Which actions are part of the basic thyroid assessment described in the lecture? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inspect the anterior neck and note visible thyroid-region size or symmetry.
Ask the patient to swallow and observe whether the thyroid region moves.
Use forceful pressure to make the gland easier to see.
Document an observed abnormality without inferring a diagnosis from appearance alone.
Skip neck inspection when the patient does not report thyroid symptoms.

questions.correct_rationale: The presentation describes thyroid inspection and observation of swallowing movement. Document visible findings objectively; the slide labels palpation and auscultation as advanced skills, so this item does not require those maneuvers.

option_rationales.A: Appropriate: inspection of the neck and thyroid region is a basic step in the described assessment.
option_rationales.B: Appropriate: the lecture identifies observation of thyroid movement during swallowing.
option_rationales.C: Not appropriate: forceful pressure is not part of inspection and may cause discomfort.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate: objective documentation communicates the finding without assigning an unsupported cause.
option_rationales.E: Not appropriate: the lecture includes neck inspection as an assessment technique, not only when symptoms are reported.

questions.exam_strategy: Keep this item to inspection and swallowing observation; the lecture labels palpation and auscultation as advanced skills.

questions.stem: The nurse palpates a firm, fixed, nontender supraclavicular node in an adult. The patient reports no recent infection. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Document the node but wait for symptoms before reporting the finding.
Repeat the examination at the next routine visit if the node remains nontender.
Describe the finding as malignant before diagnostic evaluation.
Record the node's characteristics and arrange prompt clinician evaluation.

questions.correct_rationale: A firm, fixed supraclavicular node is concerning and warrants evaluation; palpation alone cannot establish a diagnosis.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: A firm fixed supraclavicular node is concerning and should not be attributed to routine aging.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: Repeated massage cannot establish benignity and may irritate the area.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: A fixed node warrants evaluation, but palpation alone cannot prove cancer.
option_rationales.D: Best choice: Record the node's characteristics and arrange prompt clinician evaluation.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: a firm, fixed supraclavicular node is concerning and warrants evaluation; palpation alone cannot establish a diagnosis.

questions.stem: A patient with a recent sore throat has several small, mobile, tender anterior cervical nodes. The patient is afebrile and otherwise stable. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: Tenderness establishes a bacterial infection and confirms that antibiotics are needed.
A recent sore throat makes further assessment unnecessary.
The nodes may be reactive; assess the throat and follow up if they persist, enlarge, or worsen.
The nurse should diagnose malignancy because multiple nodes are palpable.

questions.correct_rationale: Tender mobile nodes after a local infection can be reactive, but the cause is not certain from palpation. Assess context and persistence.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: Tenderness can occur with inflammation but does not prove a bacterial cause or need for antibiotics.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: A recent sore throat may explain reactive nodes, but throat and associated symptoms still need assessment.
option_rationales.C: Best choice: Assess the throat and follow up if the nodes persist, enlarge, or worsen.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Palpable multiple nodes do not by themselves establish malignancy.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: tender mobile nodes after a local infection can be reactive, but the cause is not certain from palpation.

questions.stem: Which lymph-node location descriptions are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: The deep cervical chain forms a superficial midline row on the front of the neck.
Postauricular nodes are located behind the ear near the mastoid region.
Submental nodes are located beneath the chin.
Supraclavicular nodes are located above the clavicle.
Preauricular nodes are located in front of the ear.

questions.correct_rationale: The descriptions identify preauricular, postauricular, submental, and supraclavicular regions. The deep cervical chain lies deeper along the neck rather than as a visible superficial midline row.

option_rationales.A: Not appropriate: the deep cervical nodes lie along deeper neck structures, not as a visible midline row.
option_rationales.B: Appropriate: this identifies the postauricular location.
option_rationales.C: Appropriate: submental nodes are inferior to the chin.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate: the name and location refer to the area superior to the clavicle.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: the preauricular group lies anterior to the ear.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: the named groups correspond to their anatomic landmarks.

questions.stem: A patient has enlarged cervical and supraclavicular nodes and reports unexplained weight loss and drenching night sweats. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume a viral infection and advise follow-up only if the nodes become tender.
Document node distribution and characteristics, then promptly notify the clinician.
Tell the patient the findings establish lymphoma.
Massage the nodes and reassess them at a routine visit several months later.

questions.correct_rationale: Multiple enlarged nodes and constitutional symptoms need clinical evaluation; communicate observations without assigning a diagnosis.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: Supraclavicular nodes with weight loss and drenching sweats are concerning; assuming viral illness risks delayed evaluation.
option_rationales.B: Best choice: Document node distribution and characteristics, then promptly notify the clinician.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: These findings raise concern but do not establish lymphoma without further evaluation.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Massage and waiting months could delay assessment of systemic symptoms and concerning node distribution.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: multiple enlarged nodes and constitutional symptoms need clinical evaluation; communicate observations without assigning a diagnosis.

questions.stem: A patient with a rapidly enlarging anterior-neck mass develops noisy breathing and difficulty swallowing saliva. What is the priority?

options.text: Treat this as a potential airway emergency and activate immediate clinical assistance.
Complete node and thyroid palpation first so the cause is clearer.
Offer food or water to check whether the swallowing problem improves.
Arrange routine outpatient imaging and continue the assessment.

questions.correct_rationale: Noisy breathing and difficulty handling secretions with a rapidly enlarging mass can indicate airway compromise; do not delay escalation or offer oral intake.

option_rationales.A: Best choice: A rapidly enlarging neck mass with noisy breathing and inability to swallow secretions threatens the airway; activate immediate help.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: Completing palpation delays airway support in a potential emergency.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: Food or water could be aspirated when the patient cannot swallow saliva safely.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Routine imaging and continued assessment are too slow for developing airway compromise.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: noisy breathing and difficulty handling secretions with a rapidly enlarging mass can indicate airway compromise; do not delay escalation or offer oral intake.

questions.stem: Which neck findings require prompt communication or further evaluation? Select all that apply.

options.text: A new fixed supraclavicular node.
A small, mobile, mildly tender node during a short-lived URI, without other concerns.
Acute tracheal deviation accompanied by respiratory distress.
A rapidly enlarging thyroid-region mass with new dysphagia.
A new neck mass with hoarseness or other progressive compressive symptoms.

questions.correct_rationale: A fixed supraclavicular node, rapidly enlarging mass with dysphagia, tracheal deviation with distress, and progressive compressive symptoms warrant evaluation. Airway distress requires immediate escalation; a small mobile tender node during a short URI is less concerning in isolation.

option_rationales.A: Appropriate: fixation and supraclavicular location are concerning features that need clinical evaluation.
option_rationales.B: Not an urgent warning sign by itself: this may be reactive, but persistence or worsening should still be assessed.
option_rationales.C: Appropriate: airway compromise with tracheal deviation requires immediate emergency response.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate: enlargement with swallowing difficulty raises concern for compression and warrants prompt evaluation.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: progressive voice or swallowing symptoms with a mass need prompt assessment.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: fixed nodes, progressive masses with compressive symptoms, and acute respiratory distress require communication or further evaluation.

questions.stem: During neck inspection, the anterior thyroid region rises as the patient swallows. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: This is an expected observation; describe any visible asymmetry or enlargement.
The movement confirms a thyroid hormone disorder.
The movement alone does not establish enlargement or a thyroid disorder.
Press firmly on the gland during swallowing to determine the cause.

questions.correct_rationale: The lecture notes that the thyroid region moves with swallowing. The nurse should describe visible features and avoid diagnosing a thyroid disorder from movement alone.

option_rationales.A: Best choice: Thyroid movement with swallowing is an expected observation; visible size and symmetry should be described.
option_rationales.B: Movement with swallowing does not establish a hormone disorder.
option_rationales.C: Movement during swallowing alone does not establish enlargement or a thyroid disorder.
option_rationales.D: Pressing during swallowing is unnecessary and does not identify the cause of a finding.

questions.exam_strategy: Observe thyroid-region movement during swallowing and document visible size or symmetry without assigning a diagnosis.

questions.stem: While the patient is reclined, the nurse sees a soft, undulating pulsation in the neck that changes with position. Which interpretation is most likely?

options.text: A thyroid nodule, because every neck pulsation rises and falls with breathing.
A carotid bruit, which is identified by visual inspection alone.
A cervical lymph node that expands with each heartbeat.
A jugular venous pulsation; assess its position and relation to other findings.

questions.correct_rationale: A soft, undulating pulsation that changes with position is consistent with jugular venous pulsation, not an auscultated bruit or node.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: A thyroid nodule is a tissue finding, not a soft positional venous pulsation.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: A bruit is heard with a stethoscope and cannot be diagnosed by visual inspection of a pulsation.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: A lymph node does not expand and contract with each heartbeat as described.
option_rationales.D: Best choice: A soft, undulating positional neck pulsation is consistent with jugular venous pulsation and should be assessed in context.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: a soft, undulating pulsation that changes with position is consistent with jugular venous pulsation, not an auscultated bruit or node.

questions.concept: Thyroid and lymph findings in context
questions.stem: Which statements reflect safe interpretation of thyroid and lymph-node findings? Select all that apply.

options.text: The thyroid region may move with swallowing, but enlargement or compressive symptoms still need assessment.
Tenderness can occur in a reactive node but does not identify the cause by itself.
Tenderness proves that a node is bacterial and requires antibiotics.
A firm, fixed node is more concerning than a small mobile node, but palpation alone is not diagnostic.
New dysphagia, hoarseness, or breathing difficulty with a neck mass warrants prompt evaluation.

questions.correct_rationale: Interpret thyroid movement and node characteristics descriptively, not diagnostically. A firm fixed node can be more concerning than a mobile one, and dysphagia, hoarseness, or breathing difficulty with a neck mass warrants prompt evaluation.

option_rationales.A: Appropriate: movement is expected, while enlargement and symptoms require evaluation.
option_rationales.B: Appropriate: tenderness is a descriptive feature and is not specific for infection.
option_rationales.C: Not appropriate: tenderness alone cannot establish bacterial cause or justify antibiotics.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate: this distinction guides follow-up without making a diagnosis from palpation.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: these may indicate progressive compression, with breathing difficulty requiring urgent attention.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: interpret findings in context, avoid diagnosing from palpation or bruit alone, and escalate compressive symptoms.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of lymph-node removal reports slowly increasing unilateral arm swelling. Which response best applies the assessment principles from the lymphatic unit?

options.text: Assume the new swelling is cellulitis and apply heat before comparing the limbs or checking the skin.
Compare both limbs, assess swelling and skin, ask about pain, warmth, redness, and change, then arrange follow-up.
Begin forceful massage toward the chest to move fluid before assessing the affected arm.
Reassure the patient that arm swelling is inevitable after node removal and needs no further assessment.

questions.correct_rationale: Prior node removal raises the possibility of lymphedema but does not establish the cause of new unilateral swelling. Compare and characterize the finding; acute pain, warmth, redness, rapid change, or systemic symptoms would alter urgency.

option_rationales.A: Swelling has several possible causes; assess the limb and associated signs before attributing it to infection.
option_rationales.B: Best choice: It characterizes the change and checks for concerning features before appropriate clinical follow-up.
option_rationales.C: Forceful massage is not an appropriate unsupervised response to new unilateral swelling.
option_rationales.D: Lymph-node removal increases risk but does not make progressive swelling inevitable or exempt it from evaluation.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: prior node removal raises the possibility of lymphedema but does not establish the cause of new unilateral swelling.

questions.stem: A patient reports gradually worsening hearing. Which additional question best establishes onset and laterality?

options.text: Have you noticed balance changes, tinnitus, pain, drainage, or noise exposure?
Has the hearing changed gradually, or did it become worse all at once?
When did it begin, and does the change affect one ear or both?
Have any medicines changed since you first noticed the hearing problem?

questions.correct_rationale: A neutral history explores onset, laterality, associated symptoms, relevant noise/medication exposure, and functional impact without presuming infection or age-related loss.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: These related symptoms are useful, but do not establish when or on which side the change began.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: The course over time is relevant, but this question does not clarify whether one or both ears are affected.
option_rationales.C: Best choice: It directly establishes onset and laterality, two key details for characterizing gradual hearing change.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Medication history is relevant but does not establish the onset or laterality of the reported change.

questions.exam_strategy: Begin a focused hearing history by establishing when the change began and whether one or both ears are affected.

questions.stem: Which tympanic-membrane appearance is most consistent with a normal otoscopic finding?

options.text: An opaque, markedly bulging membrane with obscured landmarks.
A gray, translucent, intact membrane with visible landmarks.
A visible defect with drainage from the canal.
A bright-red membrane in every healthy adult.

questions.correct_rationale: The lecture describes a gray, translucent tympanic membrane. Color must be interpreted with landmarks, symptoms, and the full otoscopic view.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: Opacity and marked bulging with obscured landmarks are abnormal, not a normal membrane appearance.
option_rationales.B: Best choice: A gray, translucent, intact membrane with landmarks is a typical normal finding.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: A defect with drainage suggests injury or infection, not an intact normal membrane.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Healthy tympanic membranes are not expected to be bright red in every adult.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: the lecture describes a gray, translucent tympanic membrane.

questions.stem: A patient who swims frequently reports ear-canal pain that worsens when the nurse gently moves the auricle or presses the tragus. Which finding is most consistent with this pattern?

options.text: Use tragus tenderness to diagnose middle-ear infection without inspecting the canal or tympanic membrane.
Attribute the canal pain to age-related hearing loss and omit inspection because the patient swims often.
Treat pain with auricle movement as proof of a tympanic-membrane perforation, without further assessment.
Consider external-canal inflammation, then inspect the ear and interpret the finding with the history.

questions.correct_rationale: Tragus/auricle pain is associated with otitis externa but is not independently diagnostic. Continue appropriate assessment.

option_rationales.A: Tragus or auricle tenderness can support external-canal inflammation, not establish a middle-ear diagnosis.
option_rationales.B: Presbycusis does not explain pain with tragus movement; inspect the ear and assess the reported symptoms.
option_rationales.C: Auricle or tragus tenderness does not prove a membrane defect; it can occur with external-canal inflammation.
option_rationales.D: Best choice: Tragus or auricle tenderness supports an external-canal source but must be interpreted with inspection and history.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: tragus/auricle pain is associated with otitis externa but is not independently diagnostic.

questions.stem: Which statements about Rinne and Weber screening are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: In a normal Rinne pattern, air conduction is heard longer than bone conduction.
A Weber sound perceived equally in both ears is not lateralized.
Weber lateralization alone identifies the type and side of hearing loss.
A fixed two-second Rinne result proves normal hearing at every frequency.
Interpret Weber lateralization with symptoms and other findings, such as Rinne, rather than alone.

questions.correct_rationale: A normal Rinne pattern has air conduction longer than bone conduction, and equal Weber perception is not lateralized. Interpret any lateralization with symptoms and other findings; neither screening test alone establishes a complete diagnosis.

option_rationales.A: Appropriate: this is the expected normal Rinne relationship.
option_rationales.B: Appropriate: equal perception is a non-lateralized Weber result.
option_rationales.C: Not appropriate: lateralization must be interpreted with other findings and does not alone establish type and side.
option_rationales.D: Not appropriate: a bedside screening time does not establish normal hearing across frequencies.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: combined interpretation reduces overreliance on a screening result.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: rinne compares air and bone conduction; Weber lateralization must be interpreted with other findings and does not by itself identify the type of loss.

questions.stem: A tuning fork is placed at the patient's midline, and the sound is louder in the right ear. On the right, bone conduction is heard longer than air conduction. Which interpretation best fits these combined screening findings?

options.text: Consider right conductive hearing loss; correlate the screening pattern with the full assessment and further evaluation.
Conclude definite left sensorineural loss because Weber lateralizes right, regardless of the right Rinne result.
Document normal hearing in both ears because the patient detected the tuning fork at the midline.
Classify this as an equilibrium disorder because tuning-fork tests cannot screen for hearing differences.

questions.correct_rationale: Weber lateralization to the right together with bone conduction greater than air conduction on the right is consistent with possible right conductive loss. Tuning-fork tests are screening maneuvers, not a substitute for formal audiologic evaluation.

option_rationales.A: Best choice: Weber lateralization to the right with right bone conduction longer than air conduction can fit right conductive loss; screening is not definitive.
option_rationales.B: The combined findings do not prove left sensorineural loss; the right-sided Rinne pattern suggests possible conductive loss on that side.
option_rationales.C: Hearing the fork does not establish normal bilateral hearing; interpret Weber and Rinne together.
option_rationales.D: Weber and Rinne are hearing-screening maneuvers; this pattern does not assess equilibrium.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: weber lateralization to the right together with bone conduction greater than air conduction on the right is consistent with possible right conductive loss.

questions.stem: An older adult says, "I hear people talking, but I cannot understand them when the room is noisy." What is the best nursing response?

options.text: Assume difficulty understanding speech in noise is inevitable with age and do not assess further.
Tell the patient to concentrate harder in noisy rooms instead of asking about the hearing change.
Assess onset, function, exposures, medications, and communication needs; consider presbycusis without assuming it.
Test attention by speaking from another room before asking the patient about hearing or communication needs.

questions.correct_rationale: Presbycusis can affect high-frequency hearing and speech understanding in background noise, but age alone does not establish the cause. Use respectful, functional assessment.

option_rationales.A: Age-related change is possible, but the complaint still warrants assessment rather than dismissal.
option_rationales.B: This response dismisses the functional concern and does not assess onset, contributing factors, or communication needs.
option_rationales.C: Best choice: It assesses the concern and possible contributors while avoiding an age-based assumption.
option_rationales.D: Speaking from another room is not a meaningful hearing assessment and may compromise communication.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: presbycusis can affect high-frequency hearing and speech understanding in background noise, but age alone does not establish the cause.

questions.stem: A patient reports dizziness and recently fell. The nurse is considering a Romberg test. What is the safest approach?

options.text: Ask the patient to close the eyes while standing unsupported at the bed edge.
Explain the test, clear the area, guard closely, and stop if balance becomes unsafe.
Perform the test while the patient walks down the hallway.
Leave the patient alone so their balance response is natural.

questions.correct_rationale: Romberg assesses balance and requires guarding, especially with reported dizziness or a recent fall. Mild sway alone must be interpreted in context.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: Closing the eyes unsupported near a bed edge risks a fall, especially after a recent fall.
option_rationales.B: Best choice: Clearing space, explaining, guarding, and stopping when unsafe make a balance screen safer.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: Romberg is a standing balance test, not performed while walking down a hallway.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Leaving a dizzy patient with fall history unsupported creates preventable injury risk.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: romberg assesses balance and requires guarding, especially with reported dizziness or a recent fall.

questions.stem: A patient routinely inserts cotton-tipped applicators into the ear canal to remove wax. Which teaching points are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Avoid inserting objects into the ear canal because they can injure the canal or tympanic membrane.
A cotton-tipped applicator can push cerumen deeper and contribute to impaction.
Seek advice before using removal products if there is pain, drainage, sudden hearing change, or prior ear surgery.
Clean the outer ear only; do not insert the cloth or applicator into the canal.
Use a cerumen-softening product despite ear pain or prior ear surgery.

questions.correct_rationale: Keep objects out of the canal, since they can push cerumen deeper or injure the canal and tympanic membrane. Clean only the outer ear and seek advice before products when warning symptoms or prior surgery are present.

option_rationales.A: Appropriate: insertion can cause trauma and should be avoided.
option_rationales.B: Appropriate: swabs may compact wax rather than remove it.
option_rationales.C: Appropriate: these circumstances may require examination before any removal product is used.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate: external cleaning avoids canal injury and wax impaction.
option_rationales.E: Not appropriate: pain or prior ear surgery warrants advice before using an ear-canal product.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: cotton-tipped applicators can cause trauma or push cerumen inward.

questions.stem: After a sudden sharp ear pain during a flight, a patient reports drainage and reduced hearing from that ear. The nurse sees a possible tympanic-membrane defect. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Irrigate the ear canal to check the suspected membrane defect after the sudden pain and drainage.
Insert a cotton swab into the canal to estimate how deep the suspected defect may be.
Instill available ear drops now, before confirming whether the tympanic membrane is intact.
Keep the ear dry, avoid instrumentation or unverified drops, and arrange evaluation.

questions.correct_rationale: Possible perforation with pain, drainage, and reduced hearing requires evaluation. Irrigation or instrumentation can worsen injury; drops should be selected by a qualified clinician when membrane integrity is uncertain.

option_rationales.A: Irrigation is unsafe when tympanic-membrane integrity is uncertain and may worsen injury.
option_rationales.B: Instrumentation can injure the canal or membrane; do not probe a suspected defect.
option_rationales.C: Unverified drops may be inappropriate when a membrane defect is suspected; obtain clinical guidance.
option_rationales.D: Best choice: It protects the ear from further injury and arranges clinical assessment.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: possible perforation with pain, drainage, and reduced hearing requires evaluation.

questions.stem: A patient reports that one side of the nose is often blocked. Which technique best assesses nasal patency safely?

options.text: Inspect the external nose and septum, then compare airflow through each nostril while gently occluding the other.
Occlude both nostrils and ask the patient to inhale deeply to determine whether either side is patent.
Insert a cotton applicator deeply into the symptomatic nostril to estimate the passage diameter.
Diagnose a deviated septum from the report of one-sided blockage without inspecting the nose.

questions.correct_rationale: Inspect symmetry and septum, then compare patency side to side without inserting an object or diagnosing from symptoms alone.

option_rationales.A: Best choice: It compares nasal airflow safely without inserting an instrument or inferring a cause from symptoms alone.
option_rationales.B: Occluding both nostrils prevents the requested comparison and can cause unnecessary discomfort.
option_rationales.C: Deep insertion can injure nasal tissue and is not a safe way to assess patency.
option_rationales.D: Unilateral blockage has multiple possible causes; symptoms alone do not establish septal deviation.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: inspect symmetry and septum, then compare patency side to side without inserting an object or diagnosing from symptoms alone.

questions.stem: A patient reports pressure over the cheeks and forehead, nasal congestion, and tenderness with gentle sinus palpation. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: Recommend antibiotics without asking about duration or other symptoms.
Assume congestion alone establishes sinusitis without examining the nasal passages.
Consider sinus inflammation; assess duration and associated symptoms before deciding the cause.
Dismiss the tenderness as expected and omit assessment of the reported pressure.

questions.correct_rationale: Facial pressure, congestion, and tenderness are not specific for bacterial infection; treatment decisions require the full clinical picture.

option_rationales.A: Tenderness and congestion do not establish bacterial infection or an antibiotic indication.
option_rationales.B: These symptoms are nonspecific and do not establish a polyp.
option_rationales.C: Best choice: Sinus inflammation is possible, but duration and associated symptoms are needed to interpret the finding.
option_rationales.D: Tenderness with reported pressure and congestion merits assessment rather than automatic dismissal.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: facial pressure, congestion, and tenderness are not specific for bacterial infection; treatment decisions require the full clinical picture.

questions.stem: A patient reports intermittent nasal obstruction and occasional nosebleeds. Which assessment steps are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inspect the external nose for symmetry and skin changes.
Assume allergies are the cause without asking about duration, triggers, or bleeding pattern.
Ask about duration, triggers, allergies, trauma, medications, and bleeding pattern.
If bleeding is active, assess its pattern and the patient’s overall status.
Compare airflow through each nostril separately.

questions.correct_rationale: Assess nasal symmetry and patency, obtain a focused history, and evaluate the pattern and overall status during active bleeding. Do not assume allergy without evidence; assess each nostril separately as taught.

option_rationales.A: Appropriate: inspection is part of a focused nasal assessment.
option_rationales.B: Not appropriate: this presumes the cause and omits important history.
option_rationales.C: Appropriate: these details help characterize obstruction and epistaxis.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate: active bleeding requires assessment of severity and the patient’s condition.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: checking one nostril at a time helps identify unilateral or asymmetric patency.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: external inspection, one-sided patency comparison, focused history, and assessment of active bleeding support safe evaluation.

questions.stem: A patient reports nasal stuffiness and pressure over the cheeks. Which focused examination is appropriate?

options.text: Inspect the nose for symmetry and patency, then palpate the sinuses for tenderness.
Inspect the nose and test each nostril separately, then diagnose sinusitis from the result.
Compare airflow through both nostrils at once and use equal airflow to rule out obstruction.
Palpate the frontal and maxillary sinuses firmly until the exact source of pressure is clear.

questions.correct_rationale: The lecture describes inspecting the nose for symmetry and patency and palpating the sinuses for tenderness or discomfort.

option_rationales.A: Best choice: It assesses the nasal structures related to the reported stuffiness and cheek pressure.
option_rationales.B: Testing patency can be useful, but nasal airflow alone does not establish sinusitis or its cause.
option_rationales.C: Testing both nostrils together cannot identify unilateral obstruction or establish that obstruction is absent.
option_rationales.D: Excessive pressure is unnecessary; sinus palpation should be gentle and interpreted with symptoms.

questions.exam_strategy: Match the reported nasal/sinus symptoms to inspection of nasal symmetry and patency and palpation for sinus tenderness.

questions.stem: During an oral assessment, the nurse observes white patches on the buccal mucosa. Which documentation is most appropriate?

options.text: Record the location, appearance, and extent; ask about soreness and relevant oral history.
Record the site and label the cause as candidiasis based only on its color.
Compare with expected anatomy and assume the patches are normal if painless.
Ask about symptoms but omit the visible patches from the assessment record.

questions.correct_rationale: The lecture instructs learners to inspect the oral mucosa and observe white patches. Describe the finding, ask relevant symptom/history questions, and avoid diagnosing from color alone.

option_rationales.A: Best choice: It documents the visible finding and adds relevant symptom context without assuming a cause.
option_rationales.B: A color description alone does not establish candidiasis or another diagnosis.
option_rationales.C: Painlessness does not establish that a visible mucosal change is normal; describe it for interpretation.
option_rationales.D: The observed mucosal finding should be included in the assessment record.

questions.exam_strategy: Describe location and appearance of oral findings and obtain symptom context without assigning a cause.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing common oral and throat abnormalities listed in the lecture. Which term refers to inflammation of the tonsils?

options.text: Gingivitis
Tonsillitis
Thrush (candidiasis)
Gingival hyperplasia

questions.correct_rationale: Tonsillitis refers to inflammation of the tonsils; the lecture lists it among common oral/throat abnormalities.

option_rationales.A: Gingivitis is an abnormality of the gums, not the tonsils.
option_rationales.B: Best choice: Tonsillitis is the lecture-listed term for inflammation of the tonsils.
option_rationales.C: Thrush (candidiasis) is an oral finding, not inflammation of the tonsils.
option_rationales.D: Gingival hyperplasia refers to gum enlargement, not tonsil inflammation.

questions.exam_strategy: Distinguish the lecture-listed oral and throat abnormalities by the structure involved.

questions.stem: A nurse is completing an oral and throat assessment. Which actions or observations are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inspect the lips, oral mucosa, gums, teeth, tongue, and visible throat.
Note color, lesions or white patches, odor, and presence or absence of tonsils.
Assume a white patch is candidiasis without describing it or obtaining context.
Ask about pain, swallowing difficulty, oral hygiene, and relevant dental or medication history.
If the patient has stridor or cannot manage secretions, prioritize airway help over routine inspection.

questions.correct_rationale: A systematic oral/throat assessment inspects visible structures and describes findings, includes focused symptoms and history, and prioritizes airway compromise over routine inspection. A white patch should be described and interpreted in context, not diagnosed from color alone.

option_rationales.A: Appropriate: these are core parts of a systematic oral and throat inspection.
option_rationales.B: Appropriate: descriptive observations provide useful assessment data without assigning a diagnosis.
option_rationales.C: Not appropriate: white patches have multiple possible causes and require description and context.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate: focused history helps interpret oral and throat findings.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: airway compromise takes priority over a nonurgent examination.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: inspect and describe the oral/throat structures and gather focused history.

questions.stem: A client is described as having dysphagia. Which experience is most consistent with this term?

options.text: Difficulty swallowing food or liquids.
Inflammation or soreness of the gums.
A reduced sense of taste or smell.
Redness or discomfort limited to the throat.

questions.correct_rationale: The lecture defines dysphagia as difficulty swallowing.

option_rationales.A: Best choice: Dysphagia means difficulty swallowing.
option_rationales.B: Gum inflammation is not the definition of dysphagia.
option_rationales.C: A reduced sense of taste or smell is not difficulty swallowing.
option_rationales.D: Throat redness or discomfort may occur for other reasons but does not define dysphagia.

questions.exam_strategy: Recall the lecture definition: dysphagia means difficulty swallowing.

questions.stem: A patient reports recurrent sore throat and intermittent hoarseness. Which focused-history questions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask about duration, progression, fever, pain, swallowing, and voice changes.
Assume intermittent hoarseness is caused by allergy without further history.
Ask whether the patient has breathing difficulty, drooling, or inability to swallow secretions.
Ask about tobacco or irritant exposure, reflux symptoms, and relevant environmental exposures.
Ask about medication and inhaler use and any associated oral symptoms.

questions.correct_rationale: Focused history for recurrent sore throat and hoarseness includes duration, progression, airway and swallowing symptoms, exposures/reflux, and medication or inhaler use. The course supports patient-specific history rather than assuming a cause.

option_rationales.A: Appropriate: timing and associated symptoms characterize recurrent throat and voice concerns.
option_rationales.B: Not appropriate: hoarseness has multiple possible causes and should not be attributed without assessment.
option_rationales.C: Appropriate: these symptoms may indicate airway or swallowing compromise and require prompt attention.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate: these factors can contribute to throat or voice symptoms and guide assessment.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: medication and inhaler history may help interpret concurrent throat or oral findings.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: focused history includes the symptom pattern, airway/swallowing warning signs, exposures, and relevant medicines.

questions.stem: A pregnant patient reports bilateral nasal stuffiness without fever, facial pain, or purulent drainage. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Treat presumed rhinitis as bacterial sinusitis and discuss antibiotics based on congestion alone.
Assess symptoms, consider pregnancy-related congestion, and check medication safety in pregnancy.
Attribute congestion to normal pregnancy and defer assessment unless fever develops.
Suggest an over-the-counter decongestant before checking pregnancy guidance or medication history.

questions.correct_rationale: Pregnancy-related increased vascularity can contribute to congestion, but the nurse should assess the full symptom pattern and follow pregnancy-specific medication guidance rather than diagnose infection or dismiss symptoms.

option_rationales.A: Not appropriate: congestion alone does not establish bacterial sinusitis or justify antibiotics.
option_rationales.B: Best response: pregnancy-related vascular congestion is possible, but assess symptoms and verify pregnancy-specific medication safety before advising treatment.
option_rationales.C: Not appropriate: pregnancy may contribute, but waiting for fever can miss other concerning symptoms; assess the current pattern.
option_rationales.D: Not appropriate: a decongestant should not be recommended before checking individualized pregnancy guidance and medication history.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: increased vascularity in pregnancy can contribute to congestion, but the nurse should assess symptoms and avoid assuming infection.

questions.stem: Which statements about common ENMT assessment findings are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Dysphagia means difficulty swallowing.
Presbycusis can affect high-frequency hearing and speech understanding in noise.
A normal Romberg result evaluates balance and does not prove normal hearing acuity.
Weber lateralization needs interpretation with clinical context and other hearing findings.
A white oral patch is thrush whenever it is seen, without further description or assessment.

questions.correct_rationale: Dysphagia means difficulty swallowing, presbycusis can affect high-frequency hearing and speech in noise, and Weber findings need context. Oral patches should be described; color alone does not establish thrush.

option_rationales.A: Appropriate: this is the course definition of dysphagia.
option_rationales.B: Appropriate: age-related hearing loss commonly affects high-frequency perception and communication in noise.
option_rationales.C: Appropriate: Romberg assesses balance, not hearing thresholds.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate: a screening result should be considered with symptoms and complementary tests.
option_rationales.E: Not appropriate: appearance alone does not establish candidiasis; describe the finding and assess it in context.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: dysphagia is a swallowing term; presbycusis affects hearing; Weber assesses sound lateralization, while Romberg assesses equilibrium.

questions.stem: A patient walks quickly into the clinic and has a respiratory rate of 24/min while speaking. The patient is not in distress. What is the best next step?

options.text: Record the first count as the patient's resting respiratory rate.
Ask the patient to slow the breathing while the nurse counts.
Let the patient rest, then reassess rate, effort, pattern, and symptoms.
Diagnose a respiratory infection from the post-walk rate alone.

questions.correct_rationale: Recent activity can raise rate. Reassessment after rest helps establish the patient's status without coaching the breathing or diagnosing from one measurement.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: A post-exertion rate is not a resting measurement and should not be recorded as one without reassessment.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: Coaching the patient to alter breathing changes the measurement and may conceal the resting pattern.
option_rationales.C: Best choice: Rest permits a consistent reassessment of rate, effort, pattern, and symptoms.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: A transient post-walk rate alone cannot diagnose respiratory infection.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: recent activity can raise rate.

questions.stem: Which observation is most important to include during the initial inspection of an adult's anterior and posterior thorax?

options.text: Record cough history and use it as a substitute for observing current breathing.
Inspect symmetry, skin color, configuration, rate, depth, pattern, and visible effort.
Inspect only the anterior chest because posterior symmetry is not relevant.
Prioritize facial and eye features before observing respiratory effort.

questions.correct_rationale: Initial respiratory inspection directly observes the thorax and breathing pattern, while history complements but does not replace observation.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: Cough history is useful but cannot substitute for observing current thoracic and respiratory status.
option_rationales.B: Best choice: Symmetry, color, configuration, rate, depth, pattern, and effort are key initial thoracic observations.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: Posterior chest symmetry is part of respiratory inspection and should not be omitted.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Respiratory effort is the immediate focus of thorax inspection, not unrelated facial or eye features.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: initial respiratory inspection directly observes the thorax and breathing pattern, while history complements but does not replace observation.

questions.stem: While auscultating a healthy adult, the nurse hears loud, high-pitched bronchial sounds over a peripheral lung field. How should this finding be interpreted?

options.text: Diagnose pneumonia from bronchial-quality sounds at one peripheral site, without rechecking or assessing other findings.
Document bronchial-quality sounds as expected throughout the peripheral lung fields in a healthy adult.
Auscultate through clothing to soften the sound before deciding whether the peripheral finding is abnormal.
Recheck the site and compare adjacent and opposite fields; peripheral bronchial quality is unexpected and needs correlation.

questions.correct_rationale: Bronchial sounds are expected over the trachea, while vesicular sounds are expected over most peripheral lung fields. An unexpected sound location merits reassessment; it does not independently diagnose a cause.

option_rationales.A: An unexpected sound needs verification and clinical correlation; it does not by itself prove pneumonia.
option_rationales.B: Bronchial sounds are normally heard over the trachea; peripheral bronchial quality is unexpected.
option_rationales.C: Auscultation should be performed on bare skin; clothing can distort or obscure breath sounds.
option_rationales.D: Best choice: Rechecking and comparing verifies the finding before it is interpreted with the full clinical picture.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: bronchial sounds are expected over the trachea, while vesicular sounds are expected over most peripheral lung fields.

questions.stem: Which actions support a systematic lung auscultation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Listen at one posterior site and use it to represent both lungs.
Compare corresponding areas side to side in a consistent sequence.
Listen through a full respiratory cycle at each site when feasible.
Ask the patient to breathe through the mouth and pause if dizziness occurs.
Place the diaphragm on bare skin when possible.

questions.correct_rationale: Systematic auscultation uses bare skin when possible, paired side-to-side comparison, and a full cycle at each site. Ask the patient to breathe through the mouth, while pausing if dizziness occurs; do not infer both lungs from one site.

option_rationales.A: Not appropriate: one site cannot establish bilateral findings; multiple paired sites are needed.
option_rationales.B: Appropriate: paired comparison helps identify asymmetry and supports a systematic examination.
option_rationales.C: Appropriate: a full cycle allows assessment of both inspiration and expiration.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate: mouth breathing improves sound assessment; pausing reduces risk if repeated deep breaths cause dizziness.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: clothing can alter or obscure breath sounds.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: bare-skin placement, paired comparison, a full respiratory cycle, and pausing for dizziness support a systematic assessment.

questions.stem: A patient reports a persistent cough. Which follow-up question most directly characterizes its timing, quality, and sputum?

options.text: When does it occur, is it dry or productive, and what does the sputum look like?
Have medications or exposures changed since the cough began?
Is the cough accompanied by fever, shortness of breath, pain, or blood?
What makes the cough better or worse, and what have you tried?

questions.correct_rationale: The open, focused prompt characterizes cough and sputum without leading the patient or assigning a diagnosis.

option_rationales.A: Best choice: It asks directly about timing, cough quality, and sputum characteristics.
option_rationales.B: Relevant exposure history may follow, but it does not describe the cough's timing or sputum.
option_rationales.C: Associated symptoms matter, but this does not characterize the cough's quality or sputum.
option_rationales.D: Aggravating factors and prior actions are useful, but do not directly characterize timing, quality, and sputum.

questions.exam_strategy: Characterize a cough by asking about its timing, quality, and sputum; assess associated symptoms as well.

questions.stem: A patient develops a harsh, high-pitched sound during inspiration with suprasternal retractions and difficulty speaking. What is the priority response?

options.text: Finish the posterior percussion sequence before notifying the response team.
Activate emergency assistance and prioritize airway assessment.
Ask the patient to cough repeatedly and reassess after the routine exam.
Document the sound as vesicular and continue auscultation.

questions.correct_rationale: Inspiratory stridor with retractions and difficulty speaking signals potential upper-airway compromise; routine examination must not delay emergency response.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: Completing percussion delays response to inspiratory stridor, retractions, and difficulty speaking.
option_rationales.B: Best choice: Stridor with retractions and impaired speech indicates possible airway obstruction and requires emergency response.
option_rationales.C: Not selected: Repeated coughing does not address potential upper-airway obstruction and delays escalation.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Stridor is not vesicular breathing; mislabeling it and continuing routine auscultation delays emergency care.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: inspiratory stridor with retractions and difficulty speaking signals potential upper-airway compromise; routine examination must not delay emergency response.

questions.stem: Which findings indicate increased respiratory distress and require prompt reassessment or escalation? Select all that apply.

options.text: New accessory-muscle use and suprasternal retractions.
A comfortable patient speaking normally with an even pattern and no increased effort.
Inability to speak a full sentence because of breathlessness.
Markedly reduced air movement in a patient who is tiring.
New cyanosis or decreasing level of alertness.

questions.correct_rationale: Accessory-muscle use, inability to speak normally, reduced air movement with fatigue, cyanosis, and declining alertness are signs of increased respiratory distress. A comfortable patient without increased effort is a useful contrasting finding.

option_rationales.A: Appropriate: these indicate increased work of breathing and warrant prompt reassessment.
option_rationales.B: Not an indicator of increased distress: these findings are relatively reassuring, though the full assessment still matters.
option_rationales.C: Appropriate: inability to speak normally can signal significant respiratory compromise.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate: reduced air movement with fatigue can precede further deterioration and needs urgent attention.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: these suggest serious oxygenation or ventilation compromise and require immediate response.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: increased work of breathing, speech limitation, tiring with reduced air movement, and cyanosis or altered alertness warrant prompt reassessment/escalation.

questions.stem: The nurse finds increased tactile fremitus over one area of the posterior lung and hears bronchial-quality sounds in that same peripheral region. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: Diagnose pneumothorax from increased fremitus, despite the bronchial-quality sounds in the same area.
Treat bronchial-quality sounds as normal over every peripheral lung field and end the assessment.
Interpret increased fremitus as the expected finding over pleural fluid, without considering other signs.
Consider consolidation as one possibility and correlate both findings with the rest of the examination and clinical data.

questions.correct_rationale: Consolidation can increase transmission of voice sounds and produce bronchial-quality sounds peripherally. Findings need correlation and are not diagnostic in isolation.

option_rationales.A: Pneumothorax more often decreases fremitus; the combined findings do not prove it.
option_rationales.B: Bronchial-quality sounds over a peripheral field are unexpected and warrant further assessment.
option_rationales.C: Pleural fluid commonly reduces transmission of fremitus; increased fremitus can accompany consolidation.
option_rationales.D: Best choice: Increased fremitus with peripheral bronchial-quality sounds can occur with consolidation but is not diagnostic alone.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: consolidation can increase transmission of voice sounds and produce bronchial-quality sounds peripherally.

questions.stem: When percussing a healthy adult's posterior lung fields, which sound is generally expected over an air-filled lung?

options.text: Dullness, as over a fluid-filled pleural space.
Flatness, as over a large muscle.
Resonance over most air-filled lung fields.
Tympany over the entire posterior thorax.

questions.correct_rationale: Resonance is generally expected over healthy air-filled lung. Percussion should be interpreted with location and the rest of the assessment. This foundational objective is directly aligned with slide 11 and reduces duplication with #095.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: Dullness is expected over dense tissue or fluid, not most healthy air-filled lung.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: Flatness is expected over very dense tissue such as muscle, not normally aerated lung.
option_rationales.C: Best choice: Resonance is the expected percussion note over most healthy air-filled lung tissue.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Tympany is a hollow drumlike note, not the expected note over posterior lungs.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: resonance is generally expected over healthy air-filled lung.

questions.stem: Which statements about respiratory assessment findings are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wheezes can occur with narrowed airways but do not by themselves prove asthma.
Crackles may occur with fluid or reopening of small airways and need clinical correlation.
Crackles at the bases prove heart failure without considering other findings.
Decreased fremitus can occur when pleural air or fluid dampens sound transmission.
Increased fremitus can occur over consolidated lung.

questions.correct_rationale: Wheezes and crackles have multiple possible causes and require context. Decreased fremitus may occur when pleural air or fluid dampens transmission; increased fremitus may occur with consolidation. No single sound proves a diagnosis.

option_rationales.A: Appropriate: wheezing is associated with narrowed airways but is not specific to asthma.
option_rationales.B: Appropriate: crackles have several causes and should be interpreted with other findings.
option_rationales.C: Not appropriate: basal crackles are not specific and cannot establish heart failure alone.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate: air or fluid between lung and chest wall can reduce transmitted vibration.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: consolidation may transmit vocal vibrations more strongly.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: breath sounds and fremitus contribute to a pattern but do not identify every cause on their own.

questions.stem: A patient reports needing three pillows to sleep because breathing worsens when lying flat. The nurse also hears bilateral crackles and observes new ankle edema. What is the best response?

options.text: Lay the patient flat to reproduce the breathing difficulty before assessing oxygenation or vital signs.
Label the crackles as pneumonia without assessing the orthopnea, new edema, or oxygenation.
Attribute new ankle edema and positional dyspnea to aging and continue routine care without escalation.
Keep the patient upright, assess oxygenation and vital signs, and promptly communicate the combined findings.

questions.correct_rationale: Orthopnea, crackles, and new edema are a concerning cardiopulmonary pattern. Support breathing and escalate without provoking dyspnea or diagnosing a cause.

option_rationales.A: Do not provoke worsening dyspnea; maintain the position that eases breathing and assess promptly.
option_rationales.B: Crackles are nonspecific, and the combined findings require broader assessment rather than an assumed diagnosis.
option_rationales.C: New edema with orthopnea and crackles is concerning and should not be dismissed as normal aging.
option_rationales.D: Best choice: Positioning supports breathing while focused assessment and prompt communication address the concerning cluster.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: orthopnea, crackles, and new edema are a concerning cardiopulmonary pattern.

questions.concept: Severe asthma and reduced air movement
questions.stem: A patient with a history of asthma initially has loud wheezing. The patient becomes drowsy, appears exhausted, and now has very little audible air movement. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Interpret quieter wheezing as improvement and continue observation despite drowsiness and minimal air movement.
Ask the exhausted patient to walk to improve ventilation before contacting the response team.
Treat drowsiness, exhaustion, and minimal air movement as possible respiratory failure and activate emergency assistance.
Wait for the next scheduled assessment because the patient has stopped coughing and is making less noise.

questions.correct_rationale: Reduced wheeze with poor air movement and declining alertness can reflect critically reduced airflow, not recovery. Immediate response is needed.

option_rationales.A: Reduced wheezing with exhaustion and minimal air movement may signal worsening obstruction, not improvement.
option_rationales.B: Ambulation can worsen distress; the patient needs urgent assessment and assistance.
option_rationales.C: Best choice: These are signs of potentially life-threatening deterioration and require an immediate emergency response.
option_rationales.D: Less coughing or noise does not indicate recovery when air movement and alertness are declining.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: reduced wheeze with poor air movement and declining alertness can reflect critically reduced airflow, not recovery.

questions.stem: A patient with asthma wants to identify patterns that worsen symptoms. Which exposures or activities can be asthma triggers for some people? Select all that apply.

options.text: Allergens such as pollen or dust mites.
Respiratory infections.
Exercise or cold, dry air for some patients.
A trigger reported by another patient can be assumed to be this patient’s only trigger.
Tobacco smoke, other irritants, or stress for some patients.

questions.correct_rationale: Asthma triggers vary by person and may include allergens, respiratory infections, exercise or cold dry air, smoke, irritants, or stress. The course and NHLBI reference support asking about an individual pattern rather than presuming one universal trigger.

option_rationales.A: Appropriate: allergens can trigger symptoms in some people with asthma.
option_rationales.B: Appropriate: infections are a common potential asthma trigger.
option_rationales.C: Appropriate: exertion and cold dry air can trigger symptoms for some individuals.
option_rationales.D: Not appropriate: triggers vary; an individual symptom and exposure history is needed.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: irritants and stress may worsen symptoms in some people and should be explored individually.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: triggers vary.

questions.stem: On the first day after abdominal surgery, a patient has shallow breathing, reduced movement, and diminished breath sounds at both bases. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Assume diminished basal sounds are harmless after surgery and wait for fever before reassessing.
Assess oxygenation and pain, review mobility and ordered pulmonary care, and report worsening.
Diagnose postoperative pneumonia and request antibiotics without assessing oxygenation or other causes.
Keep the patient immobile to prevent discomfort, without addressing shallow breathing or reduced basal sounds.

questions.correct_rationale: Surgery, shallow breathing, and immobility increase atelectasis risk, but findings require assessment. Support prescribed pulmonary hygiene and mobility and communicate deterioration.

option_rationales.A: Diminished sounds and shallow breathing need assessment; waiting for fever may delay needed care.
option_rationales.B: Best choice: It checks key contributors, follows the prescribed plan, and communicates deterioration.
option_rationales.C: These findings alone do not diagnose pneumonia or justify antibiotics without further evaluation.
option_rationales.D: Immobility can worsen postoperative pulmonary risk; address pain and support ordered mobility and breathing measures.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: surgery, shallow breathing, and immobility increase atelectasis risk, but findings require assessment.

questions.stem: A patient has progressive dyspnea and a unilateral area of dullness with reduced breath sounds and fremitus. Imaging later identifies pleural fluid. Which statement about the assessment is most accurate?

options.text: The findings fit pleural effusion; report them for clinician evaluation and management.
Require increased fremitus to identify pleural effusion, even when breath sounds and fremitus are reduced.
Use dullness alone to diagnose infected pleural fluid without considering the full examination or imaging.
Insert a needle at the bedside to verify pleural fluid after reviewing the imaging result.

questions.correct_rationale: Effusion may produce dullness, decreased breath sounds, and decreased fremitus. These findings and imaging inform clinical care; the nurse's role is assessment and communication, not performing an unauthorized procedure.

option_rationales.A: Best choice: The pattern is compatible with pleural fluid; a clinician evaluates and determines management.
option_rationales.B: Pleural fluid can reduce fremitus; increased fremitus is not required to consider an effusion.
option_rationales.C: Dullness suggests increased density but does not identify the cause or establish infection.
option_rationales.D: Thoracentesis is an invasive procedure performed by a qualified clinician, not a nursing assessment maneuver.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: effusion may produce dullness, decreased breath sounds, and decreased fremitus.

questions.stem: A patient suddenly develops unilateral pleuritic chest pain and severe dyspnea. Which findings or actions support urgent evaluation for possible pneumothorax? Select all that apply.

options.text: Symmetric chest expansion and unchanged bilateral breath sounds in a comfortable patient.
Acute worsening oxygenation or hemodynamic instability.
Rapid emergency escalation while supporting airway and breathing.
New asymmetry in chest expansion.
Unilateral markedly diminished or absent breath sounds.

questions.correct_rationale: With sudden unilateral pleuritic pain and severe dyspnea, worsening oxygenation or instability, asymmetric expansion, or unilateral markedly reduced sounds supports urgent concern for pneumothorax. Escalate rapidly while supporting airway and breathing; do not delay for diagnostic certainty.

option_rationales.A: Not supportive of the described acute unilateral process by itself; continue clinical assessment if symptoms change.
option_rationales.B: Appropriate: deterioration suggests a time-critical emergency requiring immediate response.
option_rationales.C: Appropriate: suspected pneumothorax with severe dyspnea requires prompt escalation and stabilization.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate: new unilateral asymmetry is concerning in this acute presentation.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: this is an urgent abnormal finding in the described scenario, though not diagnostic alone.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: acute hypoxemia/instability, asymmetric expansion, and unilateral loss of breath sounds in the described scenario support urgent evaluation; emergency response must not wait for a routine exam sequence.

questions.stem: A patient reports coughing up bright-red blood and is now short of breath. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Complete the environmental history before assessing breathing.
Place the patient flat and continue the interview.
Assess airway, breathing, and oxygenation, then escalate urgently.
Reassure the patient that blood-streaked sputum is always caused by dry air.

questions.correct_rationale: Hemoptysis with dyspnea requires prompt assessment and escalation; do not delay for a complete history or make a benign assumption.

option_rationales.A: Not selected: Environmental history is secondary to immediate airway, breathing, oxygenation, and bleeding assessment.
option_rationales.B: Not selected: Lying flat can worsen breathing or aspiration risk and does not address hemoptysis with dyspnea.
option_rationales.C: Best choice: Hemoptysis with dyspnea requires immediate respiratory assessment and urgent escalation.
option_rationales.D: Not selected: Bright-red blood with dyspnea is not safely dismissed as dry air; reassurance delays urgent care.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: hemoptysis with dyspnea requires prompt assessment and escalation; do not delay for a complete history or make a benign assumption.

questions.stem: An adult's anterior-posterior chest diameter appears nearly equal to the transverse diameter. The patient has a long smoking history and prolonged expiration. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Consider a 1:1 AP-to-transverse chest diameter normal for all healthy adults, regardless of symptoms or history.
Diagnose emphysema from chest shape alone, without considering symptoms, history, or other findings.
Identify pectus excavatum from the near-equal chest diameters, without examining the chest contour.
Recognize that increased AP diameter can accompany chronic hyperinflation and correlate it with symptoms and examination.

questions.correct_rationale: A barrel-shaped chest may occur with chronic hyperinflation, but configuration alone does not diagnose emphysema.

option_rationales.A: A near-equal diameter is not typical for every healthy adult and should be interpreted in context.
option_rationales.B: Increased AP diameter can occur with chronic hyperinflation but does not independently diagnose emphysema.
option_rationales.C: Pectus excavatum is a sunken sternum; the stated finding does not establish that chest-wall deformity.
option_rationales.D: Best choice: It interprets the shape as a possible chronic finding without treating it as diagnostic by itself.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: a barrel-shaped chest may occur with chronic hyperinflation, but configuration alone does not diagnose emphysema.

questions.stem: Which statements about respiratory-rate interpretation are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: A common resting-adult reference is 12–20 breaths/minute, interpreted with symptoms and baseline.
A persistent rate near 25/minute in a resting older adult warrants assessment and context, not automatic attribution to age.
Use the adult reference range for children regardless of age.
Interpret rate with depth, pattern, effort, oxygenation, and clinical context.
Recheck an elevated or irregular rate under consistent conditions and use age-appropriate references.

questions.correct_rationale: Use an adult resting reference only as a starting point and interpret rate with age, baseline, symptoms, pattern, and effort. A persistent rate near 25 in a resting older adult warrants assessment rather than automatic attribution to age.

option_rationales.A: Appropriate: this is a common adult reference, not a stand-alone diagnosis.
option_rationales.B: Appropriate: a sustained elevation should be assessed even when age-related ranges may vary.
option_rationales.C: Not appropriate: respiratory-rate references vary by age and pediatric ranges differ.
option_rationales.D: Appropriate: rate alone does not describe respiratory status.
option_rationales.E: Appropriate: consistent measurement and age-appropriate comparison improve interpretation.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: reference ranges depend on age and assessment context.

questions.stem: A mechanically ventilated patient develops fever, purulent respiratory secretions, new crackles, and increased oxygen needs. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.text: Diagnose ventilator-associated pneumonia and identify its organism from mechanical ventilation and these symptoms alone.
Promptly evaluate for possible ventilator-associated pneumonia given the new fever, secretions, crackles, and oxygen need.
Treat fever, purulent secretions, crackles, and higher oxygen needs as expected with ventilation and do not reassess.
Exclude pneumonia because crackles are present, since pneumonia is expected to cause wheezing instead.

questions.correct_rationale: The symptom cluster warrants evaluation. Ventilation is a risk context, not by itself proof of infection, a diagnosis, or the organism.

option_rationales.A: Ventilation and symptoms do not prove pneumonia or identify a pathogen; clinical evaluation is needed.
option_rationales.B: Best choice: The new cluster is concerning for infection or another complication and warrants prompt evaluation.
option_rationales.C: These are new concerning findings, not routine effects to dismiss; reassess and communicate promptly.
option_rationales.D: Pneumonia can present with crackles; this sound does not exclude infection.

questions.exam_strategy: Use the scenario to apply this rule: the symptom cluster warrants evaluation.
